category: Comparison, similarity, contrast, opposition, and support

entries.meaning: Says two things are the same kind of thing and very far apart in quality, degree, or fidelity. It nearly always registers a disappointment: what follows the phrase is the promise, the original, or the standard, and the subject is what actually turned up.
examples: The finished building is a far cry from the drawings the council approved.
Her second album is a far cry from the bluegrass she started with.
Twelve dollars an hour is a far cry from a living wage in this county.
Running a two-person shop is a far cry from running a newsroom.
What the contractor delivered was a far cry from what the contract described.
The river is cleaner than it was in 1975, but it is still a far cry from the trout stream the old-timers describe.
entries.русский: далеко не то, что — сильно уступает обещанному или образцу, с оттенком разочарования
entries.type: complex (article + noun phrase + fixed from; wholly idiomatic — the cry is the old sense "shouting distance," so the phrase literally measures a gap)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (a far cry from hers), gerund (a far cry from running a newsroom), or a free relative (a far cry from what the contract described) — never a finite clause. It is also predicative only: it follows be, seem, or remain, and it cannot be hung on a noun as a modifier. A far cry than and a far cry to are errors; the preposition is from, exactly as in different from.
entries.pattern: [be/seem/remain] a far cry from [noun phrase] · still a far cry from [noun phrase] · a long way from — the plain paraphrase
entries.contrast: Against different from, which reports unlikeness neutrally, a far cry from measures the distance and calls it large. It is also directional: what follows the phrase is the standard, and the subject is nearly always the thing that falls short of it — the finished building is a far cry from the drawings faults the building, not the drawings. Against out of sync with, which reports a mismatch of timing or alignment, this one reports a mismatch of degree.
entries.see also: different from, unlike, in contrast to, out of sync with, the same as

entries.meaning: Says two things belong to the same family without saying they are the same thing. The adjective akin is a fossil, contracted from of kin, and outside this phrase it barely exists, which is why the whole string behaves as a single preposition.
examples: What she felt was akin to relief, though she would not have called it that.
The charge is akin to a fee for using the road.
Signing that waiver is akin to giving up the claim entirely.
He greeted the news with something akin to panic.
Their dialect is more akin to Portuguese than to Spanish.
entries.русский: сродни; близко к — того же рода, но не то же самое
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in journalism and criticism
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed preposition; marginal — akin survives almost nowhere else in modern English)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (akin to admitting defeat), or a wh-free relative (akin to what happened in 2008) — never a finite clause. Akin with is an error.
entries.pattern: be akin to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] akin to [noun phrase] · something akin to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Weaker than the same as and stronger than reminiscent of: akin to claims a family resemblance without claiming identity. Against similar to, which invites the reader to compare features, akin to is reached for when the writer wants an approximation and does not intend to defend the details — which is why something akin to is by far its commonest frame.
entries.see also: similar to, like, the same as, in common with, in the manner of

entries.meaning: Names a rough model without committing to it. The phrase is a hedge in prepositional form: whatever follows is offered as the general shape of the thing, and the speaker is explicitly reserving the right to have the details wrong.
examples: He said something along the lines of "we'll let you know Friday."
The committee wants a program along the lines of the one Ohio runs.
I was thinking along the lines of a smaller deck and a bigger porch.
They floated a settlement along the lines of what the union got in 2019.
She is looking for work along the lines of what she did before the layoff.
The state is considering a surcharge along the lines of raising the registration fee by twenty dollars.
entries.pronunciation note: also /əˈlɑŋ/ wherever cot and caught have merged · uh-long-thuh-LYNZ-uv
entries.русский: в духе; примерно как — приблизительный образец, говорящий не ручается за детали
entries.register: neutral; conversational, business, and reported speech
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (along the lines of raising the fee), a free relative (along the lines of what we did last year), or a quoted or paraphrased utterance (something along the lines of "we'll be in touch") — never a bare finite clause. Along the lines that the state would pay half is possible in formal writing, but there the that-clause is hung on the noun lines and most editors rewrite it.
entries.pattern: something along the lines of [noun phrase] · [noun] along the lines of [noun phrase] · thinking along the lines of [noun phrase] · along these/those/the same lines — adverbial, no complement
entries.variants: on the lines of is British and does not belong in American writing. Bare along those lines and along similar lines take no object at all and are adverbials, not this preposition.
entries.contrast: Against like and similar to, this phrase is deliberately approximate: it says a model is being followed loosely and declines to be pinned to the details, which is why something along the lines of is the standard American way to report words you cannot quote exactly. Against in the vein of, which places a work in an artistic tradition, along the lines of points at a plan, a proposal, or a form of words. Against in the manner of, it claims no imitation of style at all.
entries.see also: like, similar to, in the vein of, in the manner of, akin to

entries.respell: weak /əz/, and in rapid speech nearly /z/ after a vowel
entries.meaning: The comparison as asserts equality or sameness of kind: that two things measure the same, that they are the same one, or that one belongs to the set named by the other. It is among the highest-frequency words in English, and its constant traffic with the identically spelled conjunction is what makes it the hardest word in this file to use confidently.
examples: The new engine is as quiet as the old one and half the weight.
She can throw as far as anybody on the team.
He's nearly as stubborn as me — formally, as stubborn as I am.
Her schedule is exactly the same as mine.
That's the same truck as the one parked out front all week.
Root vegetables such as turnips and parsnips keep all winter in sand.
Delays such as these are unavoidable in February.
The 8:10 was late, as usual.
As always, the trailhead lot was full by seven.
Payment is due on the first, as a rule.
As many as forty families may have to move before the levee work starts.
The repair could run as much as nine thousand dollars, and that estimate is two weeks old.
The clinic sees as few as three patients on a Monday in August.
Fold the corners in, as the diagram shows.
As I said on the phone, the estimate is only good for thirty days.

senses.head: The second as of a comparison of equality
body: After a pronoun, American speech takes the objective case (as tall as me); formal writing usually restores the verb (as tall as I am).
examples: The new engine is as quiet as the old one and half the weight.
She can throw as far as anybody on the team.
He's nearly as stubborn as me — formally, as stubborn as I am.

senses.head: After the same, asserting identity of kind
examples: Her schedule is exactly the same as mine.
That's the same truck as the one parked out front all week.

senses.head: After such, introducing an example
examples: Root vegetables such as turnips and parsnips keep all winter in sand.
Delays such as these are unavoidable in February.

senses.head: Frozen adverbials of manner and expectation
examples: The 8:10 was late, as usual.
As always, the trailhead lot was full by seven.
Payment is due on the first, as a rule.

senses.head: As many as, as much as, as few as — the quantity frame
body: The correlative closes on a number, and the effect is to offer that number as a striking maximum: as many as forty means "up to forty, and forty is a lot."
examples: As many as forty families may have to move before the levee work starts.
The repair could run as much as nine thousand dollars, and that estimate is two weeks old.
The clinic sees as few as three patients on a Monday in August.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the conjunction, with a whole clause after it
body: This is the form careful writing uses where speech reaches for like.
examples: Fold the corners in, as the diagram shows.
As I said on the phone, the estimate is only good for thirty days.

entries.русский: как, в качестве; такой же, как — второй член сравнения as … as и указание на роль или тождество
entries.type: simple — the same word is also a subordinating conjunction of time, cause, and manner, the second half of the correlative as … as, and a relative pronoun after such and the same
entries.complement: in comparison, a noun phrase or an objective-case pronoun (as tall as me), and an adjective or adverb inside the correlative frame (as quickly as). It takes a finite clause only when it is doing conjunction duty (as I said), and the presence of a subject and verb after it is exactly what tells you which word you have. Never a gerund in the comparison sense, and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: as [adjective/adverb] as [noun phrase] · the same … as [noun phrase] · such … as [noun phrase] · as many/much/few/little as [quantity] · frozen adverbials: as usual, as always, as a rule, as follows
entries.variants: none. The two-word as if and as though take clauses and are conjunctions, not prepositions.
entries.contrast: Like versus as is the central rule of this file. Like takes a noun and asserts a resemblance; as names a role or heads a clause. Like your lawyer, I'd settle says the speaker is someone else who agrees with the lawyer; As your lawyer, I'd settle says the speaker is the lawyer. Before a clause, careful American prose uses as — as I said, not like I said — even though the like version is universal in speech. The role-and-capacity as (works as a nurse, regarded as unreliable) is treated with the prepositions of role at as; this entry covers as in comparison and manner.
entries.see also: like, than, similar to, the same as, as opposed to, as

entries.meaning: The workhorse expression of unlikeness, and the one that draws the most usage mail in American English. The rule that matters is short: from always works, than works and is often smoother before a clause, and to is British.
examples: Her second draft is completely different from the first.
Growing up in Fairbanks is different from anything I can describe to you.
The new packaging is no different from the old except for the color.
It tasted different from what the menu had promised.
He votes differently from the rest of his delegation on almost everything.
The building looks different than it did in the photographs — before a clause, than is the smoother choice.
entries.pronunciation note: three syllables, /ˈdɪfərənt/, in careful speech · DIF-runt frum
entries.русский: отличный от; не такой, как — стандартный предлог при different (не to, по-британски)
entries.type: complex (adjective + preposition; marginal — different is a fully live adjective, and the pair is listed here because choosing its preposition is the problem, not because the two words have fused)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (different from me), gerund (different from driving a truck), or a free relative (different from what I expected). Never a bare that-clause.
entries.pattern: [be/seem/look] different from [noun phrase] · [noun] different from [noun phrase] · no different from [noun phrase] · differently from [noun phrase]
entries.variants: different than is standard American English and is the better choice before a clause, where from forces a clumsy free relative: The house looked different than I remembered beats different from what I remembered. Different to is British and does not belong in American writing. Different from is never wrong and is the safe default.
entries.contrast: The pronoun test separates the two American forms: from is a preposition and takes the objective case (different from her), while than can be either preposition or conjunction, so different than she is and different than her are both current. Note that the verb is differ from, never differ than, and the adverb is differently from or differently than.
entries.see also: unlike, as distinct from, than, similar to, the same as, other than

entries.meaning: Marks the subject of the main clause as one more member of a group that behaves the same way. Because it is bulky and almost always fronted, it belongs to written English — a reporter writes it and nobody says it.
examples: In common with most western states, Nevada holds its primary in June.
In common with her colleagues, she had no warning that the lab would close.
The bank, in common with every lender in the state, tightened its terms that spring.
In common with many veterans of that campaign, he refused to discuss it.
In common with the older engines, this one still needs leaded fuel.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in KAH-mun with
entries.русский: как и; наравне с — подобно другим членам той же группы; книжн., только письменно
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: In common with [noun phrase], [clause] · [subject], in common with [noun phrase], [verb]
entries.contrast: Only the fronted, comma-set use is a preposition. The far commoner have something in common with is a verb plus its object plus an ordinary with-phrase, and the two cannot be swapped: In common with her sister, she plays the cello means "like her sister," while She has the cello in common with her sister means they share it as an interest. Against like, this phrase is stiffer and nearly always fronted; against along with, it asserts resemblance rather than accompaniment, and like along with it leaves the verb agreeing with the original subject alone.
entries.see also: like, akin to, similar to, along with

entries.meaning: Says the thing was made in imitation of a known style. In auction catalogues the phrase carries a specific and unflattering meaning — the work is by a follower, not the master — and that hedged quality travels with it into ordinary prose.
examples: A courtyard fountain in the manner of the Alhambra.
He wrote three novels in the manner of Dashiell Hammett and one that was entirely his own.
The sauce is finished in the manner of a classic beurre blanc.
She ran the department in the manner of a ship's captain.
The lithograph is catalogued in the manner of Daumier, which is the polite way of saying it is not one.
entries.русский: в манере; в стиле кого-л. — книжн.: подражание известному стилю, часто с намёком на копию
entries.register: formal to literary; standard in art criticism, music, and cooking
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually a proper name or a style label — never a finite clause; a gerund is grammatical but rare
entries.pattern: [noun] in the manner of [noun phrase] · [clause] in the manner of [noun phrase] · In the manner of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: after the manner of is the older and more literary form; in the style of is the plain one; the borrowed à la /ɑ ˈlɑ/ (à la Hitchcock) is informal in English. In museum and auction cataloguing, in the manner of is a term of art meaning "by an unknown follower," as against attributed to and studio of.
entries.contrast: Against like, which simply asserts a resemblance, this phrase names a deliberate imitation of a recognized style. Against as, it never assigns a role: a fresco in the manner of Giotto was emphatically not painted by Giotto, while a fresco by Giotto was.
entries.see also: like, as, akin to, in the guise of

entries.meaning: Places a work in the tradition of a named model. It is the standard shorthand of reviewing — three words that tell a reader what shelf a thing belongs on — and it commits the writer to far less than in the manner of would.
examples: It is a quiet domestic novel in the vein of Anne Tyler.
The band's third record is in the vein of early Fleetwood Mac.
He told a long story in the vein of the ones his grandfather used to tell.
The gallery wants something in the vein of what she showed in Santa Fe.
The report closes on a warning, in the vein of every county study since 1998.
She is writing satire in the vein of the eighteenth century, footnotes and all.
entries.русский: в духе; в стиле — о книге, фильме, пластинке в традиции названного образца
entries.register: neutral to formal; criticism and reviewing — books, records, films, and restaurant menus
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a proper name or a genre label (in the vein of Raymond Carver, in the vein of early punk), or a free relative (in the vein of what she showed in Santa Fe) — never a finite clause, and a gerund only awkwardly: in the vein of writing for children is grammatical and nobody writes it.
entries.pattern: [noun] in the vein of [noun phrase] · something in the vein of [noun phrase] · in a lighter/darker/similar vein, in the same vein — the adjectival frames, which take no complement at all
entries.variants: in a … vein (in a lighter vein) and in the same vein are the older constructions and are adverbials, not this preposition; in the vein of is the prepositional development of them. In the style of and in the manner of are the near-synonyms. The vein is the mining one — a seam of a particular material — not the anatomical one.
entries.contrast: Against in the manner of, which says a style was deliberately imitated, in the vein of only places a work in a tradition: a novel in the vein of Chandler need not be trying to sound like Chandler, and no forgery is implied. Against along the lines of, which points at a plan or a form of words, this points at an artistic kind. Against like, it is the reviewer's register and always names something with a recognized style attached to it.
entries.see also: in the manner of, along the lines of, akin to, like, similar to

entries.meaning: The general-purpose word of resemblance, and the busiest preposition in spoken American English. Everything it does reduces to a single operation — hold X up against Y and assert that they are alike — but the range of things that can fill those two slots is enormous, which is why the entry runs long.
examples: The new bridge looks like a harp from the river.
She drives like a professional and parks like a tourist.
Nobody else on the crew works like him.
It's not like Marcus to miss a deadline.
That is exactly like her: she paid for everyone and slipped out.
Bring something sturdy, like a tarp or a moving blanket.
Root crops like beets and carrots store well in damp sand.
The whole house smelled like woodsmoke for a week.
It felt like the first real morning of fall.
There were like forty people crammed into that kitchen.
It took like two hours just to get through security.
And she was like, "I already sent it twice."
It was, like, the third time that week — the discourse particle, with nothing after it that it governs.

senses.head: Resembling; in the same way as
examples: The new bridge looks like a harp from the river.
She drives like a professional and parks like a tourist.
Nobody else on the crew works like him.

senses.head: Typical or untypical of a person — always with be
examples: It's not like Marcus to miss a deadline.
That is exactly like her: she paid for everyone and slipped out.

senses.head: Introducing an example
examples: Bring something sturdy, like a tarp or a moving blanket.
Root crops like beets and carrots store well in damp sand.

senses.head: After verbs of perception and impression
examples: The whole house smelled like woodsmoke for a week.
It felt like the first real morning of fall.

senses.head: Approximately — informal, before a quantity
examples: There were like forty people crammed into that kitchen.
It took like two hours just to get through security.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the quotative be like and the discourse particle,
body: both conversational, neither taking an object.
examples: And she was like, "I already sent it twice."
It was, like, the third time that week — the discourse particle, with nothing after it that it governs.

entries.pronunciation note: a stressed word with no weak form, which is one reason it is so audible in American speech — LYKE
entries.русский: как; подобно; вроде — сходство; требует существительного, тогда как as вводит роль или придаточное
entries.register: neutral as a preposition; the clause-taking and approximating uses are informal
entries.type: simple — the same spelling is also a verb (I like it), an adjective (of like mind), a suffix (childlike), a quotative (he was like, no), and a discourse particle. Only the preposition takes an object and means "resembling."
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (like me, never like I), gerund (It's like driving on ice), or a wh-free relative (like what happened last year). A finite clause after like — like I said, like you told me — is informal; careful American writing uses as or as if there. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [be/look/sound/feel/smell/taste/seem] like [noun phrase] · [verb] like [noun phrase] · Like [noun phrase], [clause] · just/much/something/more like [noun phrase] · It is (not) like [person] to [verb]
entries.contrast: The like/as rule. Like takes a noun and states a resemblance; as takes a role or a clause. He works like a mule is a comparison; He works as a mule would mean the animal is his job. Before a clause, formal prose wants as (as I said) or as if (It looks as if it will rain). Against such as, some editors reserve like for resemblance and such as for actual instances (poets such as Frost), but that distinction is not observed in general American usage and like introduces examples freely.
entries.see also: as, unlike, similar to, akin to, than

entries.meaning: States a measured resemblance. It is the neutral technical alternative to like, and its natural home is a sentence in which the two things compared are of the same type and the differences are going to matter.
examples: The symptoms are similar to those of ordinary flu.
This year's model is similar to last year's except for the transmission.
Running a school board turned out to be similar to running a small business.
Her handwriting is strikingly similar to her father's.
The plan is broadly similar to one the county rejected in 2019.
entries.русский: похожий на; сходный с — нейтральный, более технический аналог like
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (similar to running a small business), or a wh-free relative (similar to what we saw last spring) — never a finite clause. Similar with and similar than are errors; the preposition is always to.
entries.pattern: [be/look/sound] similar to [noun phrase] · [noun] similar to [noun phrase] · broadly/roughly/strikingly similar to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against like, similar to is the analytic word: like asserts a likeness the reader can feel, similar to asserts one the writer could itemize, which is why lab reports and appraisals prefer it. Against the same as, it explicitly stops short of identity. Note that the noun takes different prepositions depending on the frame — a similarity to the original, but similarities between the two.
entries.see also: like, akin to, comparable to, the same as, on a par with, different from, as

entries.meaning: Names people or institutions of a recognized kind, and colors them as it does so. All three of its uses do the same grammatical work — they head a comparison class — and they differ entirely in tone, from a flat list of examples to open contempt.
examples: Grants went to the likes of Carnegie Mellon and Georgia Tech.
She has beaten the likes of three former champions this season.
The street lost the likes of the hardware store and the shoe repair within a year.
Nobody on that crew had ever seen the likes of the storm that came through in June.
There will never be the likes of her in that department again.
That club was never built for the likes of us.
He wasn't going to take advice from the likes of a night clerk.

senses.head: Such as — introducing prominent examples
examples: Grants went to the likes of Carnegie Mellon and Georgia Tech.
She has beaten the likes of three former champions this season.
The street lost the likes of the hardware store and the shoe repair within a year.

senses.head: After a negative — nothing comparable, the awe frame
examples: Nobody on that crew had ever seen the likes of the storm that came through in June.
There will never be the likes of her in that department again.

senses.head: The likes of us — the class marker
examples: That club was never built for the likes of us.
He wasn't going to take advice from the likes of a night clerk.

entries.pronunciation note: the is /ði/ before a vowel · thuh-LYKES uhv
entries.русский: такие, как; подобные — вводит примеры; в зависимости от контекста с восхищением или презрением
entries.register: neutral in the example-listing sense; the the likes of us sense is informal and rarely neutral in tone
entries.type: complex (definite article + plural noun + fixed of; the noun likes survives in almost nothing else)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (the likes of us, the likes of him), or a list of names — never a finite clause and never a gerund. The verb agrees with what follows of, not with the plural likes: the likes of Ford and GM have moved on, but the likes of Babe Ruth comes along once a century.
entries.pattern: the likes of [name or list] · never seen the likes of [noun phrase] · not for the likes of us · and the like — the fixed tail phrase, which is not this preposition and takes no object
entries.variants: the singular the like of (the like of which) is older and now chiefly formal; the likes of which is the everyday American version. And the likes of that, for "and that sort of thing," is dialectal and does not belong in writing.
entries.contrast: Against such as, which is colorless, the likes of always carries an attitude — admiration, dismissal, or awe — and it names people and institutions rather than kinds of thing: poets such as Frost, but the likes of Frost and Stevens. Against like, it is heavier and always plural in form. And note that the tone flips with the frame: after a negative it is awe (never seen the likes of it), while the likes of us and the likes of him mark a social boundary and are never neutral.
entries.see also: such as, as, like, similar to, in the vein of

entries.meaning: Says two things are one thing, or that they match in every way currently being counted. It is the plainest identity statement English has, and every error it attracts is an error in the second word.
examples: Her schedule this fall is the same as it was in the spring.
The replacement part is the same as the one that failed.
My rent is about the same as yours, and I have half the space.
We used the same contractor as the church did.
She went to the same high school as both her parents.
Saying nothing at the hearing was the same as agreeing to it.
Twenty dollars an hour here is not the same as twenty dollars an hour in Seattle.
Deferred maintenance is the same as a tax, only nobody votes on it.

senses.head: Identical to; matching in every relevant respect
examples: Her schedule this fall is the same as it was in the spring.
The replacement part is the same as the one that failed.
My rent is about the same as yours, and I have half the space.

senses.head: Split around the noun — the same [noun] as
examples: We used the same contractor as the church did.
She went to the same high school as both her parents.

senses.head: Amounting to; equivalent in effect — the evaluative use
examples: Saying nothing at the hearing was the same as agreeing to it.
Twenty dollars an hour here is not the same as twenty dollars an hour in Seattle.
Deferred maintenance is the same as a tax, only nobody votes on it.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðə ˈseɪm əz/, and in fast speech /ðə ˈseɪm z/ after a vowel — the is /ði/ before a vowel · thuh-SAME az
entries.русский: такой же, как; то же самое, что — тождество; второе слово именно as, а не that
entries.type: complex (determiner + adjective + fixed as; marginal — same is a fully live adjective, and the string is listed because choosing its second word is the problem)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (the same as me), gerund (the same as driving at night), or a wh-free relative (the same as what we had before). A finite clause can follow (the same as it always was), but there the as has gone back to conjunction duty, exactly as it does at as. Never a that-clause. The same than and the same like are errors.
entries.pattern: [be] the same as [noun phrase] · the same [noun] as [noun phrase] — the two words split around the noun · much/exactly/about/roughly the same as [noun phrase] · not the same as [noun phrase]
entries.variants: the same that in the split frame (the same house that we rented) is possible but reads as a relative clause, not as this preposition; American English uses as. Bare the same, with no complement (I'll have the same), is a noun phrase and not a preposition at all. Same as without the article (Same as last year) is idiomatic in speech and in headlines and is clipped, not wrong.
entries.contrast: The top of the likeness ladder. The same as claims identity; on a par with claims equal standing; comparable to claims that a comparison is legitimate; similar to claims a resemblance with differences left over; akin to claims only a family likeness. Against equal to, which compares amounts, the same as compares kind as well as amount — the same as a hundred dollars and equal to a hundred dollars are not quite the same claim. And note the split frame: this is the only member of the section that can put a noun between its two halves.
entries.see also: as, similar to, comparable to, equal to, on a par with, like, different from

entries.meaning: Denies a resemblance the reader might otherwise have assumed. It does the work of a whole clause in one word, and because it nearly always sits at the front of the sentence, it puts an unusually heavy burden on the complement to be the right kind of thing.
examples: Unlike her brother, she never learned to swim.
Unlike most of the coast, the peninsula gets almost no fog.
The second season, unlike the first, was filmed entirely on location.
It is unlike him to leave without saying anything.
That kind of carelessness is completely unlike her.
The sound was not unlike a train going over a trestle.
His method is not unlike the one the old county surveyor used.

senses.head: Different from
examples: Unlike her brother, she never learned to swim.
Unlike most of the coast, the peninsula gets almost no fog.
The second season, unlike the first, was filmed entirely on location.

senses.head: Uncharacteristic of a person
examples: It is unlike him to leave without saying anything.
That kind of carelessness is completely unlike her.

senses.head: Not unlike — the hedged resemblance
examples: The sound was not unlike a train going over a trestle.
His method is not unlike the one the old county surveyor used.

entries.русский: в отличие от — отрицает сходство, которое читатель мог предположить; также «не свойственно кому-л.»
entries.type: simple (historically un- + like, no longer analyzed as two pieces) — also an adjective (two unlike quantities)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (unlike me), or gerund (unlike driving in the city) — never a finite clause. Unlike I said is not English; unlike what I said is the repair.
entries.pattern: Unlike [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], unlike [noun phrase] · [be] unlike [noun phrase] · not unlike [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negative of prepositional like, and the one-word equivalent of in contrast to. The parallelism trap is worse here than anywhere else in this file because unlike is usually fronted: whatever follows it must match the subject of the main clause. Unlike the 1990s, today's market is volatile compares a decade with a market; Unlike the market of the 1990s, today's is volatile repairs it. Note the litotes not unlike, which means "rather like" and is a deliberate hedge, not a double negative to be canceled out.
entries.see also: like, in contrast to, different from, as opposed to

entries.meaning: Sets two figures or two positions opposite each other. In general prose it is a compact and slightly old-fashioned comparison word; in law it is a term of art meaning "in relation to a particular party," and there it says nothing about conflict at all.
examples: Revenue came in at $41 million as against $37 million a year earlier.
Turnout was 61 percent, as against 48 in the last off-year election.
Three inspectors now cover the whole county, as against nine in 2010.
The lien is valid as against subsequent purchasers.
The waiver has no effect as against the insurer.
Her claim is stronger as against the estate than as against the trust.

senses.head: Compared with — chiefly between two figures
examples: Revenue came in at $41 million as against $37 million a year earlier.
Turnout was 61 percent, as against 48 in the last off-year election.
Three inspectors now cover the whole county, as against nine in 2010.

senses.head: Considered in relation to; enforceable with respect to — legal
examples: The lien is valid as against subsequent purchasers.
The waiver has no effect as against the insurer.
Her claim is stronger as against the estate than as against the trust.

entries.русский: по сравнению с (о цифрах); юр. в отношении такой-то стороны — книжн.
entries.register: formal; sense 1 statistical and journalistic, sense 2 legal
entries.complement: noun phrase, very often a bare figure — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: [figure] as against [figure] · [clause] as against [noun phrase] · as against [party] — in legal use
entries.contrast: In sense 1 it is a compact compared with, and it is nearly always attached to numbers; if the sentence has no figures in it, compared with or as opposed to reads better. Sense 2 is a term of art and is not a comparison at all: valid as against third parties means "enforceable in relation to them," not "opposed to them." Against plain against, the as signals measurement rather than hostility.
entries.see also: compared with, versus, as opposed to, against, relative to

entries.meaning: Confines a rule to the parties named and to no one else. It is allocation language: the clause that follows settles who bears a loss, a cost, or a priority as between the two of them, while the outside world's rights stay untouched.
examples: As between the buyer and the seller, risk of loss passes on delivery.
The indemnity decides who pays as between the contractor and the owner.
As between the two lienholders, the bank recorded first and takes priority.
As between the partners, profits are split evenly, whatever the tax return shows.
The clause governs as between the parties only; third parties keep whatever rights they had.
The court divided the fee as between the two firms that had worked the case.
entries.русский: в отношениях между (сторонами) — юр.: правило действует только для названных сторон
entries.register: formal; legal — an American meets it in a contract's risk-allocation clause, an insurance policy, or a judicial opinion, and almost nowhere else
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming two or more parties, normally two joined by and (as between the buyer and the seller) or a plural noun (as between the partners) — never a finite clause and never a gerund. Because between is itself a preposition, a pronoun in the complement is objective: as between you and me, never as between you and I.
entries.pattern: As between [party] and [party], [clause] · [clause] as between [parties] · as between themselves
entries.variants: as among is used where there are more than two parties and a drafter wants to be exact; in practice as between covers both. Bare between, in its ordinary senses, is at between.
entries.contrast: Not a comparison. As between does not mean "compared with"; it confines a statement to the internal relations of the named parties and says nothing about anyone else. As between the buyer and the seller, the seller bears the loss allocates the loss between those two and leaves the insurer's rights exactly where they were — which is precisely why drafters use it. Against as against sense 2, which names the one party a right is good against, as between names the two parties whose relations are being fixed. Against in privity with, which asserts that a legal relationship exists at all, this one takes the relationship for granted and divides something up inside it.
entries.see also: as against, in privity with, versus, relative to, between

entries.meaning: Prices one thing below a named benchmark. It is relative-value language: nobody who uses it is interested in the absolute number, only in the size and the direction of the gap between that number and whatever is doing the measuring.
examples: The shares have traded at a discount to book value since the writedown.
Regional banks are still cheap at a discount to the sector as a whole.
The bonds were issued at a discount to par and redeemed at face value.
Closed-end funds routinely sell at a discount to net asset value.
The county sold the parcels at a discount to the appraised price to get them built on.
Its multiple sits at a fifteen percent discount to every comparable name in the index.
entries.pronunciation note: full /æt ə ˈdɪskaʊnt tu/ · at-uh-DISS-kownt too
entries.русский: с дисконтом к; дешевле, чем — фин.: ниже названного эталона цены
entries.register: formal; finance — securities analysis, earnings coverage, and appraisal, where an American meets it in a research note or on a business page
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a benchmark that carries a price or a value — a peer group, an index, book value, net asset value, par, an appraisal, a trailing average. Never a finite clause and never a gerund, and never an adjective: at a discount to cheap is not English, because the complement has to be something you could put a number on.
entries.pattern: [trade/sell/change hands/be valued] at a discount to [benchmark] · at a [figure] percent discount to [benchmark] · at a discount — adverbial, no complement
entries.variants: bare at a discount, with nothing after it, means only "below the usual price" and is an adverbial rather than this preposition. Note the two prepositions: the purchase you get cheaply takes on (a discount on the fare), while the benchmark you fall below takes to.
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of at a premium to, and the direction is the whole point: the complement is the reference, and the subject is the cheap one. The stock trades at a discount to its peers says the stock is the bargain. Against plain below, which just reports a smaller number, at a discount to implies the two are comparable assets and quietly invites a judgment about whether the gap is deserved. Against relative to, which only normalizes one quantity by another, this one states which way the gap runs.
entries.see also: at a premium to, relative to, compared with, as against, in proportion to

entries.meaning: Prices one thing above a named benchmark. It is the language of takeover bids and of anything sold on reputation, and its whole content is the gap: how far above the reference the price sits, and whether that gap is deserved.
examples: The offer values the company at a premium to Friday's closing price.
Waterfront lots sell at a premium to anything two blocks inland.
The bid came in at a thirty percent premium to the thirty-day average.
Short-dated paper is trading at a premium to the rest of the curve.
Organic milk moves at a premium to the conventional price all year.
The fund has traded at a premium to net asset value since the spring.
entries.pronunciation note: full /æt ə ˈprimiəm tu/ · at-uh-PREE-mee-um too
entries.русский: с премией к; дороже, чем — фин.: выше названного эталона цены
entries.register: formal; finance — merger coverage, securities analysis, and real estate
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a benchmark price or value — a closing price, a trailing average, a peer group, net asset value, the conventional price. Never a finite clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [trade/sell/bid/value X] at a premium to [benchmark] · at a [figure] percent premium to [benchmark] · pay a premium for [thing] — a different frame with a different preposition
entries.variants: bare at a premium, with no complement, is a separate idiom meaning "scarce and therefore dear" (parking downtown is at a premium) and has nothing to do with a benchmark. Note the two prepositions: what you pay extra for takes for (paid a premium for waterfront), while the level you exceed takes to. At a premium over is common in speech and is not wrong, but to is the house form in financial writing.
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of at a discount to, with the same directional rule: the complement is the reference, and the subject is the expensive one. Against above, which reports a bigger number and nothing more, at a premium to asserts that the two are comparable and that somebody is paying extra by choice. Against on a par with, which says the measurement came out even, it says it did not.
entries.see also: at a discount to, relative to, on a par with, compared with, over

entries.meaning: Puts the main clause beside a benchmark and invites the reader to notice the gap. Its real advantage over compared with is rhythmic: it can carry a heavy complement without stalling the sentence.
examples: By comparison with the drought years, this spring has been generous.
The fine looks trivial by comparison with what the company earned on the contract.
Our overhead is modest by comparison with firms of the same size.
By comparison with the original recording, the remaster is almost harsh.
The delay was minor by comparison with what the other agencies went through.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · by kum-PAIR-uh-sun with
entries.русский: по сравнению с — книжн., более развёрнутый вариант compared with
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-free relative (by comparison with what the company earned) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] by comparison with [noun phrase] · By comparison with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: by comparison to is equally acceptable in American English. The bare by comparison, with no complement, is an adverbial rather than a preposition: The second half was dull by comparison.
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in comparison with and slightly lighter on the page. Both are longer than compared with, which does identical work in two syllables — reach for the phrase only when the benchmark is long or when the comparison needs to be fronted.
entries.see also: in comparison with, compared with, relative to, next to

entries.meaning: Says one quantity is fitting for another — large enough, serious enough, or long enough to match it. The compensation cliché salary commensurate with experience is where most Americans meet the word, and what it means is "we will pay what your résumé justifies."
examples: Salary commensurate with experience.
The sentence should be commensurate with the harm done.
She wanted a title commensurate with the work she was already doing.
The reserve is not commensurate with the risk the fund is carrying.
Federal aid was never commensurate with the scale of the damage.
entries.русский: соразмерный; соответствующий — книжн.: величина под стать другой (зарплата по опыту)
entries.register: formal; standard in job postings, compensation policy, and sentencing
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (commensurate with what the job demands) — never a finite clause; a gerund is grammatical but rare (commensurate with running a department that size)
entries.pattern: [noun] commensurate with [noun phrase] · be commensurate with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Commensurate to is an error in current American usage; the preposition is with. Where in proportion to states an arithmetic relation, commensurate with states a judgment of fitness: a salary commensurate with experience is a fair one, not one computed from a formula. Against in line with, it is more evaluative and considerably more formal.
entries.see also: in proportion to, in line with, on a par with, comparable to, equal to, relative to

entries.meaning: Says two things are alike enough to be measured against each other. Its claim is about the legitimacy of the comparison rather than about how the comparison came out, which is exactly why appraisers, statisticians, and compensation committees reach for it.
examples: Starting salaries here are comparable to what the state pays for the same work.
The two districts are not comparable to each other in size or in wealth.
A studio in this neighborhood rents for a figure comparable to a two-bedroom upstate.
The appraiser found three recent sales comparable to the subject property.
Running the county fair is comparable to running a small hotel for a week.
This year's storm damage is comparable to what the coast saw in 2011.
Nothing in the record is comparable to the penalty the board handed down.
entries.pronunciation note: also /kəmˈpɛrəbəl/, with the stress pulled onto the second syllable — now common in American speech and still objected to by some · KAHM-pur-uh-bul too
entries.русский: сопоставимый с; сравнимый с — достаточно схожи, чтобы сравнение было правомерным
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in appraisal, statistics, and compensation
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (comparable to hers), gerund (comparable to running a small hotel), or a wh-free relative (comparable to what the coasts pay) — never a finite clause. Comparable than is an error, and comparable as is not English.
entries.pattern: [be/seem] comparable to [noun phrase] · [noun] comparable to [noun phrase] · roughly/broadly/directly comparable to [noun phrase] · not comparable to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: comparable with is the older analytic form and survives in technical writing, on the same logic that keeps compared with alive; comparable to is far commoner in American English and is safe everywhere. The related noun takes either preposition — a comparison with or a comparison to. In real-estate work the clipped noun comps (we pulled three comps) is standard and is not this preposition.
entries.contrast: Against similar to, which says two things resemble each other, comparable to says they are close enough in kind and in size that setting them side by side proves something — which is why an appraiser's comparable sale is a measurement rather than an impression. Against on a par with, it is descriptive rather than evaluative: a salary comparable to the market measures the same, while a salary on a par with the market is being judged adequate. Against the same as, it explicitly allows a gap. The negative not comparable to is the standard American way of refusing a comparison outright, and it is a stronger move than saying the two things merely differ.
entries.see also: similar to, on a par with, the same as, compared with, commensurate with, relative to

entries.meaning: Sets the main clause against a benchmark — most often an earlier period, a rival, or the alternative that was not taken. It is the commonest comparison preposition in American English and the least formal of the multi-word set.
examples: Compared to last winter, this one has been mild.
Tuition is low compared to comparable private colleges.
Our commute is nothing compared to hers.
Compared to a Broadway house, the theater is tiny.
Compared to what her parents went through, the move was easy.
A half marathon, compared to the full distance, is almost sociable.

senses.head: Measured against a benchmark or an earlier state
examples: Compared to last winter, this one has been mild.
Tuition is low compared to comparable private colleges.
Our commute is nothing compared to hers.

senses.head: Held up against something of a different kind, as a way of characterizing it — the likening use, where only to will do
examples: Compared to a Broadway house, the theater is tiny.
Compared to what her parents went through, the move was easy.
A half marathon, compared to the full distance, is almost sociable.

entries.русский: по сравнению с — самый частый вариант; также «уподобляя чему-л. другому по природе»
entries.type: complex (a fossilized past participle — it needs no subject to control it, which is what makes it a preposition rather than a dangling modifier)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (compared to me), gerund (compared to driving), or a free relative (compared to what we paid last year) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] compared to [noun phrase] · Compared to [noun phrase], [clause] · [noun] compared to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: as compared to and as compared with are heavier forms carrying no extra meaning.
entries.the traditional rule: compare to likens two unlike things (compared the city to an anthill), while compare with sets two like things side by side to weigh them (compared the 2019 figures with the 2020 figures). That distinction is real in the verb and is still worth keeping there. In the prepositional phrase, American usage has largely collapsed it and compared to now serves both jobs, with compared with surviving as the more careful choice in analytical writing. Neither is an error. What is an error is a mismatched complement: Compared to last year, sales are up is fine; Compared to last year, the company is bigger compares a year with a company.
entries.see also: compared with, in comparison with, than, relative to, versus

entries.meaning: Puts two comparable things side by side so that the difference between them can be read off. In edited American prose it is the number-against-number comparison word, which is why it dominates earnings coverage and statistical writing.
examples: The company earned $4.1 million, compared with $3.8 million a year earlier.
Compared with the coastal counties, the interior lost population.
Fuel use is down nine percent compared with the same month last year.
Compared with her earlier books, this one is tightly plotted.
The failure rate is negligible compared with the older design.
Emergency-room visits rose sharply compared with the previous quarter.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · kum-PAIRD with
entries.русский: по сравнению с — при сопоставлении однородных величин; норма газетной и финансовой прозы
entries.register: neutral to formal; the house style of most American newspapers and of financial reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a free relative (compared with what we paid last year) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] compared with [noun phrase] · Compared with [noun phrase], [clause] · [figure], compared with [figure]
entries.variants: as compared with adds length and nothing else.
entries.contrast: The analytical member of the pair. Compared with implies that the two things are of the same kind and that you are weighing the differences between them; compared to is looser and can also liken unlike things. Where a sentence carries two figures, compared with is the traditional and still-preferred choice: sales of $4.1 million, compared with $3.8 million a year ago.
entries.see also: compared to, as against, in comparison with, versus, relative to

entries.meaning: Says two quantities come out the same, or that a person or a thing is adequate to what is being asked of it. The first sense is the arithmetic one and is how contracts state amounts; the second is a fixed evaluative frame that takes a demand rather than a number.
examples: Each heir receives a share equal to one-fifth of the estate.
The deposit is equal to two months' rent.
Sales this quarter were almost exactly equal to last year's.
One hectare is equal to about two and a half acres.
Nobody was sure she would be equal to the job, and she was.
The old furnace is not equal to a winter like this one.
He proved equal to the occasion, which is more than anyone expected.

senses.head: The same in amount, value, or measure
examples: Each heir receives a share equal to one-fifth of the estate.
The deposit is equal to two months' rent.
Sales this quarter were almost exactly equal to last year's.
One hectare is equal to about two and a half acres.

senses.head: Adequate for; up to — the equal to the task frame
examples: Nobody was sure she would be equal to the job, and she was.
The old furnace is not equal to a winter like this one.
He proved equal to the occasion, which is more than anyone expected.

entries.русский: равный, равен — о величине; также «способный справиться» (equal to the task)
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in mathematics, finance, and contracts
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed preposition; marginal — equal is also a live adjective, a noun, and a verb)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (equal to hers), or a free relative (equal to what the state contributes) — never a finite clause and never a gerund. In the equal to the task frame the complement is always a noun naming a demand. Equal than is an error, and equal with survives only inside the frozen on equal terms with.
entries.pattern: [quantity] is equal to [quantity] · [payment/share] equal to [amount] · be equal to [the task / the occasion / the challenge] · equal in [respect] to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: equivalent to is the near-synonym and the better choice when two things match in value but not in kind (equivalent to three years' salary). The verb equal takes no preposition at all (the total equals nine hundred), and equate takes with or to (equating cost with quality).
entries.contrast: Against the same as, which claims identity of kind as well as of amount, equal to compares quantity and nothing else: a payment equal to one month's rent need not be rent. Against on a par with, which judges standing, it measures. Against comparable to, it reports that the measurement came out even rather than that the comparison is legitimate. And keep the two senses apart — equal to the task has stopped being arithmetic and means "adequate for."
entries.see also: the same as, comparable to, on a par with, commensurate with, in proportion to, up to

entries.meaning: Sets the main clause beside a benchmark at full length. Everything it does, compared with does in fewer syllables; what it buys in exchange is weight at the front of a sentence and room for a complement too long to trail comfortably.
examples: In comparison with the states that expanded coverage, ours has done badly.
The renovation was cheap in comparison with what a new building would have cost.
In comparison with his brother, he is practically a recluse.
Our staffing is thin in comparison with districts of the same enrollment.
The second storm was mild in comparison with the one that came through in January.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in kum-PAIR-uh-sun with
entries.русский: в сравнении с — книжн., самый длинный вариант того же сравнения
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a free relative (in comparison with what a new building would have cost) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in comparison with [noun phrase] · In comparison with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: in comparison to is equally standard in American English; with leans toward weighing two like things and to toward likening, but the two are freely interchanged. Bare in comparison is an adverbial, not a preposition.
entries.contrast: A heavier compared with and a fuller by comparison with. Where an ordinary comparative would carry the sentence — This one is cheaper — the phrase is padding, and its legitimate use is a long or fronted benchmark. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in comparison with.
entries.see also: by comparison with, compared with, relative to, in contrast to, in comparison with

entries.meaning: States that one quantity varies with another. In technical writing it means precisely that; in ordinary prose it turns up most often in the negative, where out of all proportion to is a complaint that the response did not match the provocation.
examples: Aid is distributed in proportion to enrollment, not to need.
Drag increases in proportion to the square of the speed.
Members' dues rise in proportion to revenue.
The coverage was out of all proportion to the size of the protest.
Punishment should stand in proportion to the offense, not to the offender's record.
Their share of the cost is small in proportion to the benefit they receive.
entries.русский: пропорционально; соразмерно — одна величина меняется вместе с другой
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (out of all proportion to what actually happened) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] in proportion to [noun phrase] · in direct/inverse proportion to [noun phrase] · out of (all) proportion to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in proportion with occurs but is much rarer. Out of proportion to is the standard negative form, often intensified to out of all proportion to.
entries.contrast: Against relative to, which merely normalizes one quantity by another, in proportion to asserts that the two rise and fall together — which is why it is the natural English for a mathematical relation. Against commensurate with, it is arithmetic rather than evaluative: taxes in proportion to income are calculated, taxes commensurate with income are judged fair.
entries.see also: commensurate with, relative to, in line with, according to

entries.respell: casual /ˈnɛks tə/, the medial t usually dropping
entries.meaning: Puts something beside a standard and lets the standard win. The construction is close to formulaic — Next to X, Y looks plus a judgment — and it is the most idiomatic short comparison in spoken American English.
examples: Next to her, everyone else on the panel looked unprepared.
Next to the original, the reissue sounds thin.
Next to what the coasts pay, our property taxes are nothing.
Next to a real Chicago winter, this is a mild inconvenience.
Next to his first restaurant, the new place feels corporate.
entries.русский: по сравнению с; на фоне — разг.: рядом с эталоном второе выглядит бледно
entries.complement: in the comparative sense, a noun phrase, an objective-case pronoun (next to her), or a free relative (next to what the coasts pay) — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: Next to [noun phrase], [clause] — nearly always fronted, and nearly always followed by an evaluation
entries.contrast: This entry covers only the comparative next to, "when you set it beside." The spatial sense — the pharmacy next to the hardware store — is at next to, and the limiting next to nothing and ranking next to are at next to. The comparative sense is recognizable by its position: fronted, comma-set, and followed by a clause containing a judgment. Against compared to, it is conversational and always slightly unfavorable to the thing in the main clause.
entries.see also: compared to, by comparison with, against, next to

entries.meaning: Ranks two things as equals. It is almost always deployed to defend or to dispute a claim of quality, which is why it collocates so heavily with roughly, about, and nowhere near.
examples: Their pitching staff is on a par with anybody's in the division.
The state's math scores are roughly on a par with the national average.
Our benefits package is not on a par with what the hospitals offer.
He puts that record on a par with anything the band did later.
The apprenticeship is on a par with a two-year degree in the trades.
entries.pronunciation note: casual /ɑnəˈpɑr wəθ/, the three words running together · on-uh-PAR with
entries.русский: наравне с; на одном уровне с — признаёт две вещи равными по качеству
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a free relative (on a par with what the hospitals offer) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: be on a par with [noun phrase] · [verb] on a par with [noun phrase] · roughly/about/nowhere near on a par with [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on par with — without the article — is now very common in American English and appears in edited prose, but on a par with is the traditional form and the safer one in formal writing. The financial at par, meaning "at face value," is a different expression entirely.
entries.contrast: Says the two things are of equal quality or standing, which is more than similar to (merely alike) and less than the same as (identical). Against comparable to, it is evaluative rather than measurable: a comparable salary is one you can look up, a salary on a par with the market is one being judged adequate. Note the spelling — par, from golf and from finance, never pair.
entries.see also: commensurate with, similar to, equal to, in line with, relative to

entries.meaning: Measures one quantity against another that has been chosen as the reference point. Physics gave the word its precision — motion is defined only relative to a frame — and finance borrowed it wholesale for benchmark comparisons.
examples: The fund has underperformed relative to its benchmark for three straight years.
Wages have fallen sharply relative to the cost of housing.
Relative to its population, the county has an unusual number of small airports.
Velocity is meaningless except relative to a chosen frame of reference.
Our defect rate is low relative to the industry, and still falling.
The dollar strengthened relative to every major currency last quarter.
entries.русский: относительно; по отношению к — по сравнению с выбранной точкой отсчёта; фин., науч.
entries.register: formal; standard in finance, physics, and statistics
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a free relative (relative to what the coasts pay) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] relative to [noun phrase] · Relative to [noun phrase], [clause] · [noun] relative to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The normalizing comparison word: relative to implies that the benchmark is being used to scale the first quantity, not merely to sit beside it. Wages fell relative to housing costs says the ratio moved; Wages fell compared with housing costs is looser about what actually happened. The unrelated bureaucratic sense "concerning" — questions relative to the timeline — is stiff English for about and is treated with the complex prepositions at relative to; in the comparison field only the quantitative sense is live.
entries.see also: in proportion to, compared with, in comparison with, vis-à-vis, relative to

entries.respell: weak /ðən/, and in fast speech a syllabic /ðn̩/
entries.meaning: The comparison word proper. Everything else in this file names a benchmark; than attaches directly to a comparative and completes it, which is why it cannot be dropped and cannot be moved. It is also, in exactly the same shape, a conjunction, and the whole difficulty of the word lies in telling the two apart.
examples: The second offer was better than the first by about nine thousand dollars.
She got there faster than anyone expected.
He's a good deal taller than me now.
Fewer than two hundred of these were ever built.
There was nothing on the table other than a jar of pennies.
He'd rather drive all night than pay for a motel.
No sooner had the tarp gone up than the wind took it.
She cited Learned Hand, than whom no American judge is more quoted.
He likes the dog more than I do.
The trip cost more than we had budgeted for the whole quarter.

senses.head: After a comparative adjective or adverb
examples: The second offer was better than the first by about nine thousand dollars.
She got there faster than anyone expected.
He's a good deal taller than me now.

senses.head: After more, less, fewer, other, rather, else
examples: Fewer than two hundred of these were ever built.
There was nothing on the table other than a jar of pennies.
He'd rather drive all night than pay for a motel.

senses.head: The frozen frames
body: No sooner … than takes a clause; than whom is the one place where the preposition is unmistakable.
examples: No sooner had the tarp gone up than the wind took it.
She cited Learned Hand, than whom no American judge is more quoted.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the conjunction, with a clause after it
body: Restoring the verb also settles any question about who is doing what.
examples: He likes the dog more than I do.
The trip cost more than we had budgeted for the whole quarter.

entries.pronunciation note: the weak form is the normal one, and the strong form appears only under emphasis or in citation · THAN / thun
entries.русский: чем — присоединяет второй член сравнения после сравнительной степени (taller than me — выше меня)
entries.type: simple — and this is the whole problem: than is also a subordinating conjunction, spelled and pronounced identically
entries.complement: as a preposition, a noun phrase or an objective-case pronoun (taller than me); as a conjunction, a finite clause (taller than I am) or a clause reduced by ellipsis. A free relative also works (more than what we budgeted). The fixed than whom is always prepositional and always objective. Never a that-clause, and never a bare infinitive except in the two frozen frames rather than (chose to walk rather than wait) and would rather … than (I'd rather walk than wait) — note that no sooner … than takes a finite clause, not an infinitive.
entries.pattern: [comparative adjective/adverb] than [noun phrase] · [comparative] than [clause] · more/less/fewer [noun] than [noun phrase] · other than, rather than, no sooner … than, no less a figure than [noun phrase], than whom
entries.contrast: Preposition or conjunction — the test is what follows it. A bare noun makes it a preposition and calls for the objective case: She's faster than me. A clause makes it a conjunction, and the pronoun is that clause's subject: She's faster than I am, or by ellipsis She's faster than I. Both are correct English; than I with no following verb sounds stiff in American speech but is standard in formal writing. Ambiguity is the real reason to care — He likes her more than me and He likes her more than I mean different things, and restoring the verb (more than I do) is the fix. Keep than apart from then. And note that different than is standard American (see different from) while superior than, inferior than, and prefer … than are errors: those words take to.
entries.see also: as, different from, rather than, compared to, other than

entries.meaning: States where one thing stands when it is set opposite another. Diplomacy and economics keep it alive because it names a relative position — of a currency, a bargaining party, an institution — without committing to a number or to a quarrel.
examples: The dollar has weakened vis-à-vis the euro for six straight months.
Nobody has explained the university's position vis-à-vis the union.
Our costs are high vis-à-vis the rest of the industry.
The treaty leaves the smaller states with little leverage vis-à-vis their neighbors.
Vis-à-vis the previous administration, the shift is one of tone rather than of policy.
entries.pronunciation note: both written s letters are silent · veez-ah-VEE
entries.русский: по отношению к; в сравнении с — книжн., из фр. «лицом к лицу»; о взаимном положении сторон
entries.register: formal, and faintly self-conscious in American prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] vis-à-vis [noun phrase] · Vis-à-vis [noun phrase], [clause] · [noun] vis-à-vis [noun phrase]
entries.variants: vis-a-vis and vis à vis both appear; the grave accent is optional in American text and the hyphens are standard. All spellings are pronounced alike.
entries.contrast: Not a synonym for versus. Versus sets two parties in conflict; vis-à-vis only positions one thing in relation to another and is neutral about whether they are fighting. Against relative to, it is less quantitative and more political — it is the standard word for one party's standing with respect to another. Its separate "concerning, with regard to" sense is treated with the prepositions of topic at vis-à-vis.
entries.see also: relative to, versus, as against, vis-à-vis

entries.meaning: Sets one thing in opposition to another — in argument, in a contest, or as a measuring stick. All the senses below share a single geometry, two things facing each other, and they differ only in whether the facing is hostile, competitive, evaluative, or merely visual.
examples: Every member of the delegation voted against the bill.
Her lawyer advised against saying anything publicly.
Two of the three commissioners came out against the rezoning.
The Wolverines play against a ranked opponent for the third week running.
She ran against an incumbent and lost by four hundred votes.
The peso lost ground against the dollar.
Check the transcript against the recording before you file it.
Earnings are up nine percent against the same quarter last year.
The clinic vaccinates against four strains.
We're insured against flood but not against wind.
Black branches against a white sky.
Her voice stood out against the noise of the platform.

senses.head: In opposition to a proposal, a person, or a course of action
examples: Every member of the delegation voted against the bill.
Her lawyer advised against saying anything publicly.
Two of the three commissioners came out against the rezoning.

senses.head: In competition with
examples: The Wolverines play against a ranked opponent for the third week running.
She ran against an incumbent and lost by four hundred votes.

senses.head: Measured or checked against a standard
examples: The peso lost ground against the dollar.
Check the transcript against the recording before you file it.
Earnings are up nine percent against the same quarter last year.

senses.head: As protection or insurance from
examples: The clinic vaccinates against four strains.
We're insured against flood but not against wind.

senses.head: Seen with something behind it — the visual backdrop, where the contrast is what makes the thing visible
examples: Black branches against a white sky.
Her voice stood out against the noise of the platform.

entries.pronunciation note: also /əˈɡeɪnst/, a minority American pronunciation and commoner in British English — uh-GENST / uh-GAYNST
entries.русский: против; вопреки; на фоне — противостояние, состязание или сверка с эталоном
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (argued against raising the fee), or a free relative (against what the committee recommended) — never a finite clause. Write against the claim that he knew, not against he knew.
entries.pattern: [verb] against [noun phrase] · [noun] against [noun phrase] · as against [noun phrase] · stranded: the amendment she voted against
entries.contrast: This entry covers against in opposition, competition, and benchmarking. Its physical senses — forcible contact (hail against the skylight), leaning (a bike against the fence), and motion into a force (rowing against the current) — are treated with the prepositions of movement at against. Against versus, which is a labeling word joining two names, against is the ordinary verb-governed preposition: teams play against each other, but the marquee reads Ohio State versus Michigan. Against opposed to, it is shorter and less deliberative.
entries.see also: versus, in opposition to, as against, counter to, up against, against

entries.meaning: Declares the speaker on the opposite side of something. It is one of a very small number of English prepositions that are also live prefixes, and in the United States the prefix has all but crowded out the preposition.
examples: He's been anti the whole redevelopment scheme from the start. (informal, British-flavored)
Nobody in that department is anti technology exactly — they just want training first.
She isn't anti unions; she's anti this particular contract.
Anti-tax groups spent heavily on the referendum. (prefix — the normal American form)
Are you pro or anti? (no object — here it is an adjective, not a preposition)
entries.pronunciation note: the /aɪ/ pronunciation is the American default and the /i/ one is heard in British English and in some fixed compounds · AN-ty / AN-tee
entries.русский: против — разг.; в американском английском почти всегда приставка анти-, а не самостоятельный предлог
entries.register: informal, and chiefly British as a preposition; American English uses the hyphenated prefix (anti-tax, anti-union) or the ordinary preposition against
entries.type: simple (marginal — from the Greek preposition; in American English it is overwhelmingly a prefix, and its free-standing prepositional use is rare)
entries.complement: noun phrase only, with or without a determiner (anti unions, anti the whole idea) — never a clause, never a gerund. Note that anti is also a noun (the antis picketed the hearing) and an adjective (Are you pro or anti?), and in neither of those does it take an object.
entries.pattern: be anti [noun phrase] · anti- [noun] as a prefix — the American norm · pro or anti — predicative, no object
entries.variants: American style hyphenates the prefix before a proper noun or a capital (anti-American) and closes up long-established combinations (antifreeze, antibiotic, antitrust).
entries.contrast: The mirror of pro, and the two behave identically. Both are genuinely prepositional only in casual speech and both are more current in British English in that use. In American prose the natural choices are opposed to or against: She is against the merger, not She is anti the merger.
entries.see also: pro, against, in opposition to, counter to

entries.meaning: Marks a boundary between two things that habitually get run together. It is the workhorse of definitions and of any argument whose first move is to say what is not being claimed.
examples: We are talking about market value as distinct from replacement cost.
The statute governs custody as distinct from visitation.
She studies how people vote, as distinct from what they tell pollsters.
Chronic pain, as distinct from the acute kind, rarely responds to that class of drug.
This is a question of etiquette as distinct from one of law.
entries.русский: в отличие от; в противоположность — книжн.: разграничивает два смешиваемых понятия
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a free relative (as distinct from what they tell pollsters) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] as distinct from [noun phrase] · [clause], as distinct from [noun phrase]
entries.variants: as distinguished from is the legal and philosophical form and means exactly the same thing; as opposed to is the everyday equivalent.
entries.contrast: Its job is to head off a confusion the reader might otherwise fall into, so its complement is always something the first item could plausibly be mistaken for. Against as opposed to, which usually carries a preference, as distinct from is purely taxonomic — it draws a line without taking a side. Against rather than, which rejects one of two options, it keeps both and merely separates them.
entries.see also: as opposed to, in contrast to, rather than, other than

entries.meaning: Names the alternative you are not talking about, so the reader knows which of two readings to take. Its complement must be grammatically parallel to the thing contrasted with it — that parallelism is the whole discipline of the phrase.
examples: We're hiring a contractor, as opposed to a full-time employee.
The problem is structural as opposed to cosmetic.
She wanted to be judged on the work, as opposed to on who recommended her.
He took the train as opposed to driving, which added two hours.
This is a recommendation as opposed to a requirement.
As opposed to the coastal route, the inland highway stays open all winter.
entries.русский: в отличие от; а не — называет тот вариант, о котором речь как раз не идёт
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (as opposed to waiting), or an adjective or prepositional phrase parallel to whatever precedes it (careless as opposed to malicious) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [X] as opposed to [Y] · [clause], as opposed to [noun phrase] · As opposed to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: opposed to without as is a predicative adjective (I am opposed to the plan) — a different construction with a different job, since that one states the speaker's position while this one contrasts two options.
entries.contrast: The everyday form of as distinct from, and unlike it this one usually carries a preference: whatever comes after as opposed to is the rejected option. That is the exact reverse of in favor of, where what follows is the option that won. Against rather than, which is nearly interchangeable, as opposed to more often clarifies a category and rather than more often reports a choice. Against instead of, which substitutes one thing for another, as opposed to only contrasts them.
entries.see also: rather than, as distinct from, in contrast to, in favor of, instead of

entries.meaning: Says two parties are locked in a quarrel that is going nowhere. Reporters reach for it when the news is not that a disagreement exists but that it has hardened, which is why the phrase so often arrives with a stretch of time attached.
examples: The mayor has been at loggerheads with the council since the budget vote.
Two trustees remain at loggerheads with the rest of the board over the endowment.
The union is at loggerheads with management on scheduling and on nothing else.
She spent a decade at loggerheads with the agency she now runs.
The two states are at loggerheads with each other over water rights that were supposed to be settled in 1922.
Both departments were at loggerheads with the contractor by the time the slab was poured.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈlɑɡərhɛdz/ wherever cot and caught have merged · full /æt/ · at-LOG-ur-hedz-with
entries.русский: на ножах с; в затяжной ссоре с — разг./газетн., о зашедшем в тупик конфликте
entries.register: neutral; journalistic — a headline and lead-paragraph phrase more than a conversational one
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person, a group, or an institution — never a finite clause and never a gerund, and, unlike at odds with, never a document, an account, or a set of figures: his testimony is at loggerheads with the log is wrong, and the repair is at odds with. The subject of the quarrel is named with over, not with a second with.
