entries.pattern: be at loggerheads with [person/body] · be at loggerheads over [issue] · the two sides are at loggerheads — adverbial, no complement
entries.variants: at loggerheads with no complement is the commonest form of all (the two agencies have been at loggerheads all year) and is an adverbial rather than this preposition. There is no singular at loggerhead; the noun is a seventeenth-century word of disputed origin and never appears here in the singular.
entries.contrast: The vivid cousin of at odds with, and narrower in two ways. At odds with covers people and evidence alike; this one covers only parties. And at loggerheads with adds deadlock: the quarrel has been running a while and neither side is moving, which is why it collocates so heavily with have been and remain. Against in opposition to, which states a position formally taken, this reports a state of relations.
entries.see also: at odds with, at variance with, in opposition to, up against, against

entries.meaning: Says two things fail to fit together. What is at odds may be two people who cannot agree or two accounts that cannot both be true, and English uses one phrase for both.
examples: The governor has been at odds with her own party since the special session.
He found himself at odds with every other member of the committee.
The two agencies are at odds with each other over who pays for the cleanup.
His testimony is at odds with the security footage.
The policy is at odds with everything the company says publicly.
That figure is badly at odds with the county's own estimate.

senses.head: In conflict with a person or a body
examples: The governor has been at odds with her own party since the special session.
He found himself at odds with every other member of the committee.
The two agencies are at odds with each other over who pays for the cleanup.

senses.head: Inconsistent with a fact, an account, or a principle
examples: His testimony is at odds with the security footage.
The policy is at odds with everything the company says publicly.
That figure is badly at odds with the county's own estimate.

entries.русский: в разладе с; не согласуется с — о ссорящихся людях и о противоречащих друг другу сведениях
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a free relative (at odds with what the audit found) — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: be at odds with [noun phrase] · [noun] at odds with [noun phrase] · at odds over [topic] — the subject of the quarrel takes over, not with
entries.variants: at odds alone, with no complement, means the parties disagree with one another: The two agencies have been at odds all year.
entries.contrast: Against at variance with, which is formal and used almost exclusively of statements and data, at odds with covers both people and evidence and is at home in a newspaper. Note the two prepositions in a single frame: you are at odds with a person over an issue, and swapping them is the usual error.
entries.see also: at variance with, inconsistent with, contrary to, counter to, consistent with

entries.meaning: Reports that two accounts, records, or results fail to agree. It survives chiefly because auditors, judges, and scientists need a neutral way of saying that two things which ought to match do not.
examples: The invoice totals are at variance with the shipping records.
His account of the meeting is at variance with the minutes.
The finding is at variance with every earlier study of the same population.
The building as constructed is at variance with the approved drawings.
Nothing in her statement is at variance with what the other witnesses said.
entries.русский: расходится с; не согласуется с — книжн., юр. и науч.: два документа или результата не сходятся
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (at variance with what the other witnesses said) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: be at variance with [noun phrase] · [noun] at variance with [noun phrase]
entries.variants: none. In land-use law a variance is a permitted exception to a zoning rule and has nothing to do with this phrase.
entries.contrast: The formal twin of at odds with, and narrower: it is used of statements, records, and measurements, and only rarely of people. Against inconsistent with, it is more literary; against contrary to, it reports a mismatch rather than an act of defiance.
entries.see also: at odds with, inconsistent with, contrary to, consistent with, in accordance with

entries.meaning: Asserts that one thing contradicts another — a rule, an instruction, an expectation, or a widely held belief. It is stronger than difference: something contrary to the forecast does not merely differ from it, it shows the forecast to have been wrong.
examples: The valves were installed contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
He acted contrary to the advice of every lawyer in the room.
The ruling runs contrary to forty years of practice in this circuit.
Contrary to popular belief, most avalanches are triggered by their victims.
Contrary to what the brochure implies, the shuttle runs only twice a day.
Contrary to expectations, the smaller school won by nineteen.

senses.head: In conflict with a rule, an instruction, or an expectation
examples: The valves were installed contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
He acted contrary to the advice of every lawyer in the room.
The ruling runs contrary to forty years of practice in this circuit.

senses.head: The corrective opener — unlike what people generally assume
examples: Contrary to popular belief, most avalanches are triggered by their victims.
Contrary to what the brochure implies, the shuttle runs only twice a day.
Contrary to expectations, the smaller school won by nineteen.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable; the unrelated adjective meaning "perverse" is /kənˈtrɛri/, kun-TRAIR-ee · KAHN-trair-ee too
entries.русский: вопреки; в противоречие с — не просто отличие, а опровержение правила или ожидания
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (contrary to what the ads say) — never a that-clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: Contrary to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], contrary to [noun phrase] · run contrary to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: none. Evidence to the contrary and on the contrary are fixed phrases built on the noun contrary, not on this preposition.
entries.contrast: Against in contrast to, which merely sets two things side by side, contrary to asserts that one contradicts the other: in contrast to the forecast means the weather differed from it, while contrary to the forecast means the forecast was wrong. Against counter to, which is nearly identical, contrary to is the commoner and slightly more formal. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at contrary to.
entries.see also: counter to, in contrast to, at odds with, in accordance with, contrary to

entries.meaning: Says that one thing works in the opposite direction from another. The metaphor is mechanical rather than moral, which makes it the natural word for evidence that cuts against a hypothesis.
examples: The findings run counter to thirty years of received wisdom.
That policy runs counter to everything the agency was set up to do.
Counter to expectations, enrollment held steady.
Nothing in the report is counter to the union's position.
Selling into a panic runs counter to every instinct, which is exactly why it works.
entries.русский: вразрез с; в противоположном направлении от — метафора механическая, а не моральная
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (counter to what the data show) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: run counter to [noun phrase] · fly counter to [noun phrase] · [be/act] counter to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Almost always used with run: run counter to is the collocation, and the bare counter to expectations is a shortening of it. Against contrary to, it is a shade more physical, as if two forces were moving in opposite directions; against in defiance of, it implies no intent at all, since a fact can run counter to a theory without meaning anything by it. Distinguish the verb counter (she countered the objection) and the adverb (the current runs counter), neither of which governs an object with to.
entries.see also: contrary to, at odds with, in defiance of, against

entries.meaning: Concedes a fact that would normally have prevented what the main clause reports. It subordinates that fact rather than balancing it, so whatever sits in the despite phrase is the obstacle and the main clause carries the point.
examples: Despite the rain, the game started on time.
She got the job despite having no formal training.
The bridge held despite decades of deferred maintenance.
He kept his voice level despite being furious.
Despite everything that had happened that year, they stayed friends.
The bill passed despite the fact that no one had read it.
entries.русский: несмотря на — уступка: названное обстоятельство должно было помешать, но не помешало
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (despite knowing better) — never a finite clause. To put a clause after it you must expand to despite the fact that.
entries.pattern: Despite [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] despite [noun phrase] · despite [verb-ing] · despite the fact that [clause]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in spite of in every context; despite is simply shorter, which is why editors prefer it. Despite of is always an error — it is a blend of the two, and it is the single most common mistake made with this word. Against notwithstanding, which is heavier, legal in flavor, and uniquely able to follow its object (the objections notwithstanding); despite can only precede. Against regardless of, which means "without taking into account" rather than "even though" — she was hired regardless of her experience says experience was not considered, while despite her experience says it counted against her. Note that the concessive conjunctions although and even though take the finite clause that despite refuses: see although.
entries.see also: in spite of, notwithstanding, regardless of, contrary to

entries.meaning: Sets its object against the main clause as the opposite case and warns the reader in advance to expect a difference. The two halves have to be the same kind of thing, or the sentence collapses into a false comparison.
examples: In contrast to the coasts, the interior stayed dry all summer.
Her second novel, in contrast to the first, is almost cheerful.
In contrast to what the survey found, actual turnout was lowest among the youngest voters.
The northern district gained population, in contrast to every other part of the state.
In contrast to earlier models, this one runs almost silently.
Enrollment rose here, in contrast with a statewide decline of four percent.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun contrast is stressed on the first syllable; the verb contrast is /kənˈtræst/, kun-TRAST · in KAHN-trast too
entries.русский: в отличие от; в противоположность — прямо противопоставляет два однородных предмета
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a free relative (in contrast to what the survey found) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: In contrast to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], in contrast to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in contrast with is equally standard in American English. Bare in contrast, with no complement, is a conjunctive adverb rather than a preposition: Sales fell. In contrast, margins improved. In contrast of is an error.
entries.contrast: Against unlike, which is one word and does the same work, in contrast to is heavier and likelier to be fronted for emphasis. Against contrary to, it makes no claim that either side is mistaken — it only reports a difference. The parallelism rule is strict here: In contrast to the 1990s, today's market is volatile compares a decade with a market. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in contrast to.
entries.see also: unlike, as opposed to, contrary to, by comparison with, in contrast to

entries.meaning: Says the act was done knowingly against an authority, an order, or a warning. It is a strong word and a judgment, which is why careful reporters spend it sparingly.
examples: The vessel sailed in defiance of a Coast Guard order.
They kept the clinic open in defiance of the injunction.
In defiance of every forecast, the incumbent won going away.
The mural went up overnight in defiance of the historical commission.
She published the memo in defiance of a direct instruction from counsel.
entries.русский: вопреки; в нарушение — сделано сознательно наперекор приказу, запрету или предупреждению
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund, though the noun phrase is far commoner — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in defiance of [noun phrase] · In defiance of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Unlike contrary to and counter to, this phrase attributes intent: you act in defiance of an order only if you knew about it. Against in violation of, which is the neutral legal statement that a rule was broken, in defiance of characterizes the actor's attitude. Against notwithstanding and despite, which merely concede an obstacle, it asserts deliberate refusal.
entries.see also: counter to, contrary to, in opposition to, notwithstanding, in spite of

entries.meaning: the older phrase leans toward in defiance of, because the noun despite originally meant contempt — in despite of the law meant "in scorn of it," not merely "even though it existed." Against in spite of, which is the same phrase worn smooth and now purely concessive, in despite of keeps the sting.
examples: He held the pass in despite of every order to withdraw.
The charter was confirmed in despite of the abbot's protest.
She kept the old spelling in despite of her editors — a deliberate period joke in a modern sentence.
In despite of wind and tide, they made the harbor before dark.
In despite of Fortune, the family prospered another eighty years.
He married her in despite of his father; a modern writer would say despite his father's objections.

senses.head: In defiance of; in scorn of — the older and stronger sense
examples: He held the pass in despite of every order to withdraw.
The charter was confirmed in despite of the abbot's protest.
She kept the old spelling in despite of her editors — a deliberate period joke in a modern sentence.

senses.head: Concessive: even though — the sense that survived into modern despite
examples: In despite of wind and tide, they made the harbor before dark.
In despite of Fortune, the family prospered another eighty years.
He married her in despite of his father; a modern writer would say despite his father's objections.

entries.русский: наперекор; несмотря на — устар., книжн.: старая полная форма despite (Шекспир, старые тексты)
entries.register: nobody writes it today without meaning to sound old.
entries.type: complex (the ancestor of the one-word despite, which is what was left after the frame wore away)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. In older texts the complement is very often a person or a personified force (in despite of Fortune, in despite of the abbot), and that is a good clue that the older, stronger sense is meant.
entries.pattern: in despite of [noun phrase] · in despite of [person] — the older "in scorn of, to the vexation of" frame
entries.variants: the modern equivalents are despite and in spite of. Note that despite of — the phrase with in dropped — is an error in modern English, and the reason writers keep producing it by accident is that it is a half-memory of this genuine older form. Middle English also had the bare maugre, now wholly obsolete.
entries.contrast: Two things separate it from modern despite.
entries.see also: despite, in defiance of, in the teeth of, in spite of, notwithstanding

entries.meaning: Names what an act, a document, or a movement is set against. It is the standard caption language of American motion practice — every Opposition to Motion to Dismiss is one — and it carries that deliberative weight into ordinary prose.
examples: Plaintiffs filed a brief in opposition to the motion for summary judgment.
Three council members spoke in opposition to the variance.
In opposition to the leadership, a dozen members voted with the minority.
The letter was signed by sixty economists in opposition to the tariff.
She organized in opposition to the highway extension for eleven years.
entries.русский: против; в противовес — книжн., юр. и полит.: то, чему акт или документ противопоставлен
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in opposition to raising the cap) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in opposition to [noun phrase] · In opposition to [noun phrase], [clause] · [document] in opposition to [motion]
entries.variants: in opposition alone is a standing political phrase (the party in opposition) and is not this preposition.
entries.contrast: The formal counterpart of against and the exact mirror of in support of. It is the register of filings and floor speeches: a brief is filed in opposition to a motion, but a neighbor simply speaks against the permit. Against the predicative adjective opposed to, which describes a person's standing position, this phrase attaches to an act.
entries.see also: in support of, against, anti, in defiance of, in favor of

entries.meaning: Says the thing was done straight into whatever was resisting it. The phrase comes off a sailing ship, and the picture of a vessel driving to windward is still faintly present every time it is used of a vote, a boycott, or a body of evidence.
examples: The bill passed in the teeth of the strongest lobbying campaign in years.
She won the seat in the teeth of her own party's leadership.
In the teeth of the evidence, he went on insisting the numbers were fine.
They rebuilt the pier in the teeth of two more storms that winter.
The little boat beat north in the teeth of a February gale.
The crew worked all night in the teeth of forty-knot winds.

senses.head: Against active opposition or contrary evidence — the ordinary modern use
examples: The bill passed in the teeth of the strongest lobbying campaign in years.
She won the seat in the teeth of her own party's leadership.
In the teeth of the evidence, he went on insisting the numbers were fine.
They rebuilt the pier in the teeth of two more storms that winter.

senses.head: Straight into the wind — the literal nautical original
examples: The little boat beat north in the teeth of a February gale.
The crew worked all night in the teeth of forty-knot winds.

entries.русский: наперекор; прямо навстречу — книжн., образн.: против ветра, сопротивления, очевидных фактов
entries.register: formal to literary; still live in journalism, where it is a heightened alternative to in the face of
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a force that is pushing back — a gale, a boycott, an injunction, resistance, the evidence. Never a finite clause and never a gerund: in the teeth of knowing better is not English. The complement must be capable of opposing something, which is why in the teeth of a mild afternoon is nonsense while in the teeth of a February gale is not.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the teeth of [noun phrase] · In the teeth of [noun phrase], [clause] · in the teeth of the wind/the gale — the original nautical frame
entries.variants: in the face of is the plain modern equivalent and is far commoner; in the teeth of keeps the picture of a headwind. There is no singular in the tooth of, and into the teeth of is a phrase of movement, not this one.
entries.contrast: Against despite, which merely concedes an obstacle, in the teeth of insists the obstacle was actively resisting — the metaphor is a boat beating to windward. Against in defiance of, which attributes an intent to disobey some authority, this attributes only persistence against a force, and the force need not be anybody's decision. Against in the face of, it is stronger and a shade literary, and it is the only one of the three that still works literally, of wind.
entries.see also: in the face of, in defiance of, despite, against, up against

entries.meaning: Says two things cannot both be true, or that one does not square with the other. It is the standard American negative in law, medicine, and audit, and its whole usefulness is that it identifies a conflict without characterizing anybody's conduct.
examples: His statement is inconsistent with the timeline in the dispatch log.
The injuries are inconsistent with a fall.
Nothing in the deposition is inconsistent with what she told the police that night.
The reading is inconsistent with everything the other sensors recorded.
Any provision inconsistent with federal law is void.
The board's practice has been inconsistent with its own written policy for years.
State rules apply except to the extent they are inconsistent with the collective bargaining agreement.

senses.head: Not reconcilable with an account, a record, or the evidence
examples: His statement is inconsistent with the timeline in the dispatch log.
The injuries are inconsistent with a fall.
Nothing in the deposition is inconsistent with what she told the police that night.
The reading is inconsistent with everything the other sensors recorded.

senses.head: Not reconcilable with a rule, a policy, or a governing instrument
examples: Any provision inconsistent with federal law is void.
The board's practice has been inconsistent with its own written policy for years.
State rules apply except to the extent they are inconsistent with the collective bargaining agreement.

entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in-kun-SISS-tunt with
entries.русский: несовместимый с; противоречащий — книжн.: два утверждения не могут быть верны одновременно
entries.register: formal to neutral; legal, medical, scientific, and administrative
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (inconsistent with what the witness told police) — never a finite clause; a gerund is possible but rare. Inconsistent to and inconsistent from are errors — the preposition is with.
entries.pattern: be inconsistent with [noun phrase] · [noun] inconsistent with [noun phrase] · wholly/materially/facially inconsistent with [noun phrase] · to the extent inconsistent with [instrument] — the contract formula
entries.variants: none. Distinguish the ordinary adjective inconsistent meaning "erratic" (an inconsistent pitcher), which takes no complement at all, and the noun inconsistency, which takes in (an inconsistency in the record) or between (inconsistencies between the two accounts).
entries.contrast: The exact negative of consistent with, and it inherits that phrase's modesty in reverse: it says two things cannot both be right and stops short of saying which one is wrong. Against contrary to, which claims that one side contradicts a rule or an expectation, inconsistent with reports a clash between two accounts and assigns no blame. Against at odds with, it is the more analytic and the likelier in a brief; against at variance with, it is far commoner in American English and covers people as well as records.
entries.see also: consistent with, at odds with, at variance with, contrary to, in violation of

entries.meaning: Places one thing facing another, literally or figuratively. Of the three constructions that share this shape, only the abstract "reverse of" sense is fully American; the other two either prefer across from or drop the to altogether.
examples: The drug had an effect exactly opposite to the one intended.
Her conclusions are opposite to his in every particular.
The current runs opposite to the prevailing wind along this stretch.
The pharmacy is opposite to the courthouse. (British; American: across from the courthouse)
She sat opposite him for two hours and said nothing. (bare — standard American)
He played opposite Katharine Hepburn in three pictures.
She was cast opposite an actor she had never met.

senses.head: The reverse of — abstract, and the live American sense
examples: The drug had an effect exactly opposite to the one intended.
Her conclusions are opposite to his in every particular.
The current runs opposite to the prevailing wind along this stretch.

senses.head: Facing; across from — spatial. Here opposite to is British and Americans say across from or bare opposite
examples: The pharmacy is opposite to the courthouse. (British; American: across from the courthouse)
She sat opposite him for two hours and said nothing. (bare — standard American)

senses.head: As the co-star of — theater and film, always bare
examples: He played opposite Katharine Hepburn in three pictures.
She was cast opposite an actor she had never met.

entries.русский: противоположный чему-л. — обратное по смыслу; в значении «напротив» американцы говорят across from
entries.register: formal; in the spatial sense opposite to is chiefly British, and American English says across from or bare opposite
entries.type: complex — though the bare preposition opposite, with no to, is the ordinary American form
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: [noun] opposite to [noun phrase] · [noun/clause] opposite [noun phrase] — the bare American form · play/star opposite [person]
entries.variants: bare opposite (the house opposite ours, she sat opposite him) is standard in both varieties and is the normal American choice; opposite from is nonstandard; across from is the everyday American spatial equivalent.
entries.contrast: Three different things share this shape. The spatial opposite means "facing," and Americans usually say across from. The abstract opposite to means "the reverse of" and is fully current in American writing — an effect opposite to the one intended. The theatrical opposite means "as the co-star of" and never takes to at all. Against in front of, opposite requires the two things to face each other; against contrary to, it describes a relation rather than a conflict. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at opposite to.
entries.see also: contrary to, in contrast to, in front of, opposite to

entries.meaning: Reports that two things which ought to be moving together are not. What has gone wrong is timing or alignment rather than truth, which is why the phrase covers an audio track, a bus schedule, and a politician's instincts with no change of meaning.
examples: The bus schedule is out of sync with the ferry, and always has been.
Their pay scale has fallen badly out of sync with the rest of the region.
The audio drifts out of sync with the picture about ten minutes in.
He sounded out of sync with his own party for the first time in years.
The council's priorities are wildly out of sync with what people said at the hearings.
Planting dates are increasingly out of sync with the last frost.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌaʊd ə ˈsɪŋk wəθ/, the medial t flapping and of reducing to a single vowel — owt-uv-SINK with
entries.русский: не в такт с; рассогласован с — разг.: сбой в синхронности или согласованности, а не в истинности
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversational and journalistic
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a free relative (out of sync with what people said at the hearings) — never a finite clause and never a gerund. Out of sync with running the meeting is not English; write out of sync with the way the meeting is run.
entries.pattern: [be/fall/get/drift] out of sync with [noun phrase] · badly/wildly/increasingly out of sync with [noun phrase] · out of sync — adverbial, no complement
entries.variants: out of synch with is an accepted spelling and is losing ground. Out of step with is the near-synonym and is the better choice where the mismatch is one of politics or opinion rather than of timing.
entries.contrast: The everyday member of the mismatch family, and the one that survives best in speech. Against inconsistent with, which says two accounts cannot both be true, out of sync with says only that two things are not moving together — a schedule, a market, a mood. Against at variance with, it is not a finding: nobody writes it in an audit. Against at odds with, it implies no quarrel, only drift. Its positive is in sync with, which is treated with the prepositions of alignment.
entries.see also: in sync with, at odds with, inconsistent with, at variance with, in line with

entries.meaning: Names the obstacle the subject has to get past. It is the idiom of tight deadlines, long odds, and better-funded opponents, and it carries a note of strain that plain against does not.
examples: We're up against a Friday deadline and two people are out sick.
You have no idea what she was up against that first year.
Small growers are up against buyers who set the price.
The campaign came up against a spending limit it had not planned for.
After the second surgery they were really up against it.
entries.русский: перед лицом чего-л.; столкнуться с — разг.: препятствие, которое надо преодолеть
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a finite clause, never a gerund. The idiom up against it, meaning "in serious trouble," takes only the fixed pronoun it.
entries.pattern: be up against [noun phrase] · come up against [noun phrase] · be up against it — fixed idiom
entries.contrast: Where against names an opponent neutrally, up against casts the subject as the underdog: We're playing against Central is a schedule, We're up against Central is a warning. The literal spatial up against the wall, meaning touching it, belongs with the contact senses of against; in the sense treated here the object is always an obstacle, a deadline, or a stronger opponent.
entries.see also: against, at odds with, in the face of, against

entries.meaning: Names the two sides of a contest, a case, or a choice. It is a labeling word rather than a sentence word — it can join two nouns with no verb anywhere in sight, which is exactly what headlines, dockets, and marquees need.
examples: The regional final is Lincoln versus Grant, and it will be sold out.
The Court's decision in Miranda v. Arizona is more than half a century old.
It came down to the union versus the city, with the state watching.
The whole debate is speed versus accuracy.
She had to weigh a bigger salary versus another two years of training.
Renting versus buying looks very different at these rates.
What matters is what the policy covers versus what people think it covers.

senses.head: Against, in a contest or a lawsuit
examples: The regional final is Lincoln versus Grant, and it will be sold out.
The Court's decision in Miranda v. Arizona is more than half a century old.
It came down to the union versus the city, with the state watching.

senses.head: As opposed to — a choice between two options or two framings
examples: The whole debate is speed versus accuracy.
She had to weigh a bigger salary versus another two years of training.
Renting versus buying looks very different at these rates.
What matters is what the policy covers versus what people think it covers.

entries.русский: против; в противовес — в состязаниях, судебных делах и при выборе из двух (сокр. vs., v.)
entries.register: neutral; the abbreviations are the usual written forms
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a bare one with no determiner (quality versus quantity). It joins two parallel constituents of almost any kind — nouns, gerunds, adjectives, even prepositional phrases — and in headlines and titles it frequently joins them with no verb in the sentence at all. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [X] versus [Y] · [X] vs. [Y] · [case name] v. [case name]
entries.variants: vs. is the general abbreviation and takes a period in American usage (Yankees vs. Red Sox); v. is reserved for the names of court cases (Brown v. Board of Education), where it is read aloud as "versus," or by many lawyers as "against" or simply "and." AP style uses vs.; some sports usage drops the period.
entries.contrast: Not a synonym for vis-à-vis. Versus asserts conflict or an either/or choice, while vis-à-vis only names a relative position. Against against, versus is a labeling word rather than a verb-governed preposition: you play against a team, but the poster reads Duke versus Kentucky. Against as opposed to, it is more schematic — it frames a clean binary, which is why it dominates headlines and slide titles. In running formal prose, spell it out rather than abbreviating.
entries.see also: against, as opposed to, as against, vis-à-vis, rather than

entries.meaning: Names the option that was passed over. It is stiffer than rather than and much stiffer than over, and its natural home is a policy document or a formal recommendation.
examples: The committee chose the smaller site in preference to the riverfront parcel.
Use the hex bolts in preference to the screws that came in the box.
She was appointed in preference to two more senior candidates.
Most readers still take the printed edition in preference to the app.
The state funded rail in preference to widening the interstate.
entries.русский: предпочтительнее, чем; вместо — книжн.; после него стоит отвергнутый вариант
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [choose/use/appoint X] in preference to [Y] · [clause] in preference to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Note that the verb prefer takes to, not than: prefer coffee to tea, never prefer coffee than tea. With infinitives, rather than is the idiom: I'd prefer to walk rather than wait. In preference to is the noun-phrase form of the same idea; against in favor of, it is about taste rather than about dropping one option to take up another.
entries.see also: rather than, over, in favor of, instead of

entries.meaning: Ranks one thing above another. In every sense below two candidates are in play and over names the winner, whether the contest is a decision, a legal claim, a chain of command, or a scoreboard.
examples: She took the teaching job over two offers that paid more.
The board picked the local firm over a national one.
Voters chose the bond measure over a sales-tax increase by nine points.
Secured creditors are paid over everyone else.
Seniority gives him first claim over the summer shifts.
Safety takes priority over the schedule, and it says so on the wall.
She has three supervisors over her and nobody under her.
Congress has no authority over a state's ballot design in that respect.
The Tigers took a four-run lead over Cleveland in the fifth.
The alloy's advantage over steel is weight, not strength.
The canoe went over in the first set of rapids — adverb, no object.
Read it over once more before you sign, and then the whole thing is over — particle, then adjective.

senses.head: Chosen in place of — after a verb of choosing
examples: She took the teaching job over two offers that paid more.
The board picked the local firm over a national one.
Voters chose the bond measure over a sales-tax increase by nine points.

senses.head: Ahead of, in rank or in claim
examples: Secured creditors are paid over everyone else.
Seniority gives him first claim over the summer shifts.
Safety takes priority over the schedule, and it says so on the wall.

senses.head: In authority above
examples: She has three supervisors over her and nobody under her.
Congress has no authority over a state's ballot design in that respect.

senses.head: Superiority in a contest or a measurement — the margin sense
examples: The Tigers took a four-run lead over Cleveland in the fifth.
The alloy's advantage over steel is weight, not strength.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the adverb, the verb particle, and the adjective
body: None of these takes an object, which is exactly what separates them from the four senses above.
examples: The canoe went over in the first set of rapids — adverb, no object.
Read it over once more before you sign, and then the whole thing is over — particle, then adjective.

entries.pronunciation note: a stressed word with no weak form; the clipped o'er /ɔr/ is poetic only — OH-vur
entries.русский: предпочесть чему-л.; выше, над — выбор в пользу первого, а также превосходство в ранге или счёте
entries.type: simple — also an adverb (it tipped over), a verb particle (think it over), an adjective (the game is over), and a noun in cricket
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (chose settling over going to trial), or a free relative (over what the state was offering) — never a finite clause. The preposition always has an object; the adverb and the verb particle never do (it tipped over, think it over), and that is the test for which word you are looking at.
entries.pattern: [choose/pick/prefer/take/select X] over [Y] · [advantage/edge/lead/priority/claim] over [noun phrase] · [verb of authority] over [noun phrase] · not prepositional: [verb] over with no object
entries.contrast: This entry covers only over in preference and precedence. Its spatial senses are at over, its duration sense at over, and its "subject of a quarrel" sense at over. In the preference sense it competes with rather than and instead of: over needs two noun phrases and a verb of choosing, rather than can take verbs as well, and instead of implies substitution rather than ranking. Note that the verb prefer traditionally takes to (prefer tea to coffee), though prefer X over Y is now common in American English and is no longer worth objecting to.
entries.see also: rather than, in preference to, in favor of, ahead of, over

entries.meaning: Names the option that was turned down. It is the most flexible of the preference words because it accepts a noun, a gerund, or a bare infinitive; the price of that flexibility is that its complement has to be matched carefully to whatever precedes it.
examples: She asked for time off rather than a raise.
Rather than a fine, the court imposed community service.
The delay was a supply problem rather than a labor problem.
Rather than waiting for the ferry, we drove around the bay.
He chose to resign rather than answer the committee's questions.
The company would close the plant rather than renegotiate.
The dispatcher, rather than the drivers, decides the route.
Cost, rather than safety, was the reason given.

senses.head: Instead of, in place of — before a noun phrase
examples: She asked for time off rather than a raise.
Rather than a fine, the court imposed community service.
The delay was a supply problem rather than a labor problem.

senses.head: Before a verb — gerund or bare infinitive, matching whatever precedes it
examples: Rather than waiting for the ferry, we drove around the bay.
He chose to resign rather than answer the committee's questions.
The company would close the plant rather than renegotiate.

senses.head: Appended to a subject — the verb still agrees with the subject alone
examples: The dispatcher, rather than the drivers, decides the route.
Cost, rather than safety, was the reason given.

entries.русский: а не; вместо того чтобы — называет отвергнутый вариант; берёт имя, герундий или инфинитив
entries.type: complex — and grammatically a hybrid: it behaves as a preposition before a noun phrase and as a coordinator before a verb
entries.never a finite clause: rather than he should go is not English.
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (rather than waiting), bare infinitive when a to-infinitive precedes it (chose to walk rather than wait), adjective, or prepositional phrase — whatever is parallel to the item being contrasted.
entries.pattern: [X] rather than [Y] · Rather than [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause] · [subject], rather than [noun phrase], [singular verb] · would rather [bare verb] than [bare verb] — a separate construction
entries.variants: instead of is the near-equivalent before nouns and gerunds but cannot take a bare infinitive: rather than wait is fine, instead of wait is not.
entries.contrast: Verb agreement. Like as well as and along with, this phrase does not build a compound subject: The manager, rather than the clerks, is responsible. Parallelism governs the complement: whatever follows must match the form of what precedes it — to drive rather than fly, driving rather than flying, never a mixture of the two. And keep it apart from the split frame would rather … than, in which the two words are separated and both verbs are bare: I'd rather walk than wait.
entries.see also: instead of, as opposed to, over, in preference to, than

entries.meaning: Says two things can both be true at once, or that a thing fits a known pattern. The whole value of the phrase is its modesty: it claims compatibility and stops there, which is precisely what an expert witness or a radiologist needs it to do.
examples: The bruising is consistent with a fall from that height.
Her account is entirely consistent with the timeline in the dispatch log.
The readings are consistent with a slow leak rather than a rupture.
Please continue to act consistent with the policy until the board revises it.
Nothing we found is consistent with an electrical cause.
The award is consistent with what arbitrators have done in similar cases.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · kun-SISS-tunt with
entries.русский: согласуется с; совместимо с — мед., юр.: не противоречит и укладывается в известную картину
entries.register: formal to neutral; heavily used in medicine, law, and engineering
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a free relative (consistent with what arbitrators have done) — never a finite clause. Consistent to is an error.
entries.pattern: be consistent with [noun phrase] · [noun] consistent with [noun phrase] · findings/injuries/results consistent with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negatives are inconsistent with and at odds with. Against in accordance with, which reports obedience to a rule, consistent with reports only that two things do not conflict — which is exactly why the medical formula injuries consistent with a fall is so carefully weak: it says the evidence fits that story, not that the story is true. Against in keeping with, it is analytic rather than evaluative.
entries.see also: inconsistent with, in accordance with, in keeping with, in line with, at variance with, at odds with

entries.meaning: States that an act conformed to a governing rule, standard, or instrument. It is compliance language, and in ordinary prose under, following, or as required by is nearly always the better choice.
examples: The audit was conducted in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards.
Ballots will be counted in accordance with state law.
The device must be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications.
In accordance with your instructions, we canceled the order on Friday.
Benefits are calculated in accordance with the schedule in Appendix B.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in uh-KOR-dunss with
entries.русский: в соответствии с; согласно — книжн., юр.: действие отвечает норме или предписанию
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in accordance with what the statute requires) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] in accordance with [noun phrase] · In accordance with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: in conformity with, in compliance with, and the one-word pursuant to are the near-synonyms of the same register; under and as required by are the plain-English replacements. In accordance to is an error, and so is in accordance of.
entries.contrast: In accordance to is always an error — the noun accordance takes with. Against according to, which reports what a source says, this reports conformity to a rule: According to the manual, the valve closes (the manual says so) versus The valve was installed in accordance with the manual (the installation followed it). Against in keeping with, it binds — rules require accordance, traditions only invite keeping. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in accordance with.
entries.see also: in keeping with, in line with, consistent with, contrary to, according to

entries.meaning: States that a thing was made, done, or drawn up to match a governing standard. It is the auditor's and the code official's word, and in ordinary prose under, following, or as required by nearly always reads better.
examples: The statements were prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
All wiring must be in conformity with the state electrical code before the meter goes in.
In conformity with the settlement, the district rewrote its discipline policy over the summer.
The trustees distributed the residue in conformity with the terms of the will.
Nothing about the addition is in conformity with what the historic district requires.
The samples were collected in conformity with the protocol filed with the agency.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in kun-FOR-muh-tee with
entries.русский: в соответствии с; сообразно — книжн., юр. и бухг.: сделано по установленному стандарту
entries.register: formal; legal, regulatory, and accounting — an American meets it in an auditor's report, a building code, a consent decree, or a will
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in conformity with what the code requires) — never a finite clause and never a gerund. In conformity with installing the meter is not English: the complement names the standard, never the act being measured against it.
entries.pattern: [clause] in conformity with [rule/standard/instrument] · In conformity with [noun phrase], [clause] · prepared/audited/constructed in conformity with [standard]
entries.variants: in conformity to occurs and is not an error, but with is far commoner in American English; the bare noun takes either (conformity with the statute, conformity to type). In conformity of is an error. The near-synonyms of the same register are in accordance with, in compliance with, and pursuant to; under and as required by are the plain-English replacements.
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in accordance with in nearly every sentence, and a shade stiffer. Against in compliance with, which reports that a specific obligation was discharged, in conformity with reports that a thing matches a standard's shape — which is why an accountant's statements are prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles rather than in compliance with them. Against consistent with, which claims only that nothing conflicts, it claims positive agreement. Its negative is the noun phrase nonconformity with, not a preposition.
entries.see also: in accordance with, in line with, in keeping with, consistent with, contrary to, pursuant to

entries.meaning: Names what is being protected or argued for. Something has to be under threat for the phrase to make sense — a reputation, a flock, a championship — and that requirement is what separates it from the other support prepositions.
examples: He wrote a long letter in defense of the department's record.
She spoke in defense of a colleague nobody else would defend.
In defense of the old system, it never once lost a file.
The dog was shot in defense of the flock.
Two firefighters were injured in defense of the outbuildings.
She returns to Melbourne in January in defense of her title.
The team travels to Denver in defense of a nine-game winning streak.

senses.head: Arguing or acting to protect something under attack
examples: He wrote a long letter in defense of the department's record.
She spoke in defense of a colleague nobody else would defend.
In defense of the old system, it never once lost a file.

senses.head: Physically protecting
examples: The dog was shot in defense of the flock.
Two firefighters were injured in defense of the outbuildings.

senses.head: Defending a title or championship
examples: She returns to Melbourne in January in defense of her title.
The team travels to Denver in defense of a nine-game winning streak.

entries.русский: в защиту кого/чего-л. — предполагает, что объект под угрозой или подвергся нападкам
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (in defense of doing nothing) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in defense of [noun phrase] · In defense of [noun phrase], [clause] · in [possessive] defense — the short alternative frame
entries.variants: in defence of is the British spelling; American English uses defense. The possessive frame in her defense is idiomatic and far commoner than in defense of her. Note the stress: the sports noun meaning "the defending side" is /ˈdifɛns/, DEE-fenss, but inside this phrase the stress stays on the second syllable.
entries.contrast: Against in support of, which backs a proposal, in defense of answers an attack — there has to be a criticism, a charge, or a threat somewhere in the picture. Against on behalf of, it implies no authorization: you may defend someone who never asked you to. In athletics, in defense of the title means the holder is trying to keep it.
entries.see also: in support of, on behalf of, in favor of, on the side of, for

entries.meaning: Declares approval of something, names the option that won a choice, or assigns a benefit. All three senses turn on the same idea of favor, but they attach to very different kinds of sentence and are easy to run together.
examples: Nine members voted in favor of the measure.
Are you in favor of moving the meeting to Thursday?
Public opinion has shifted sharply in favor of the plan.
The city dropped the streetcar plan in favor of dedicated bus lanes.
She turned down the corporate offer in favor of a research fellowship.
The court ruled in favor of the tenants.
Make the check payable in favor of the trust, not the individual.

senses.head: Supporting; approving of
examples: Nine members voted in favor of the measure.
Are you in favor of moving the meeting to Thursday?
Public opinion has shifted sharply in favor of the plan.

senses.head: Chosen in place of — the surviving option follows the phrase
examples: The city dropped the streetcar plan in favor of dedicated bus lanes.
She turned down the corporate offer in favor of a research fellowship.

senses.head: To the legal or financial benefit of
examples: The court ruled in favor of the tenants.
Make the check payable in favor of the trust, not the individual.

entries.русский: в пользу; за — одобрение; выбранный вариант; юр. в чью-либо пользу
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (in favor of raising the cap) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: be in favor of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · vote in favor of [noun phrase] · [drop/abandon X] in favor of [Y] · rule/decide/find in favor of [party]
entries.variants: in favour of is British; American English drops the u. In X's favor is the possessive alternative: the ruling went in her favor.
entries.contrast: Three senses a reader has to keep apart. Sense 1 is approval, the opposite of against. Sense 2 is preference, and here the thing after the phrase is the option that won — the exact reverse of as opposed to, where what follows is the option rejected. Sense 3 is legal and financial and means "to the benefit of." Against plain for, sense 1 is the deliberative register: I'm for it in the hallway, I am in favor of the amendment on the record. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in favor of.
entries.see also: in support of, in opposition to, on the side of, over, in favor of

entries.meaning: Says the act fits the tone or the precedent of whatever came before it. It is evaluative rather than regulatory, which is why it collocates so strongly with tradition, spirit, character, and wishes.
examples: In keeping with tradition, the outgoing chair gave the closing toast.
The addition is in keeping with the character of the block.
In keeping with the family's wishes, the service was private.
His decision was entirely in keeping with everything he had said publicly.
The raise is in keeping with what neighboring districts have offered.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in KEE-ping with
entries.русский: в духе; в соответствии с — согласуется с традицией, характером или волей кого-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in keeping with what neighboring districts have offered) — never a finite clause; a gerund is grammatical but awkward
entries.pattern: [clause], in keeping with [noun phrase] · In keeping with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Where in accordance with means conformity to a rule that binds, in keeping with means consistency with a spirit, a tradition, or a character — nobody is obliged. In accordance with the statute is legally required; in keeping with the family's wishes is fitting but optional. In line with sits between the two, and consistent with is the analytic version of the same idea. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in keeping with.
entries.see also: in line with, in accordance with, consistent with, in the manner of, in keeping with

entries.meaning: Reports that something matched a forecast, a policy, or a standard. It is the standard verb-free way for analysts and reporters to say "as predicted," and bring into line with is its transitive twin.
examples: Third-quarter results came in in line with analysts' forecasts.
Wage growth is now roughly in line with inflation.
In line with company policy, expenses over fifty dollars need a receipt.
The new rules bring the state in line with federal standards.
The proposal is broadly in line with what the committee recommended.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in LYNE with
entries.русский: в соответствии с; совпадает с — о результате, совпавшем с прогнозом, планом или нормой
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in line with what the committee recommended) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] in line with [noun phrase] · In line with [noun phrase], [clause] · bring/come/fall in line with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Weaker than in accordance with, which implies obligation, and more quantitative than in keeping with, which is about spirit: earnings come in in line with expectations, but a memorial service is in keeping with someone's wishes. Keep the frozen phrase apart from the literal in line with the doorframe, meaning physically aligned, which uses the same three words. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in line with.
entries.see also: in keeping with, in accordance with, consistent with, on a par with, in line with

entries.meaning: Says two parties stand in a legal relationship close enough to carry rights and duties between them. Whether privity exists is the threshold question in a whole class of American lawsuits, and the phrase is almost always doing that work — deciding who is allowed to sue whom.
examples: The subcontractor was never in privity with the owner and has to sue the general contractor instead.
Most states have dropped the rule that a buyer must be in privity with the manufacturer to bring a warranty claim.
The insurer is not in privity with the repair shop and cannot enforce the estimate against it.
The tenant is in privity of estate with the landlord for as long as the lease runs.
Because the assignee stands in privity with the original lessee, the covenant runs with the land.
The court held that the second plaintiff was not in privity with the first, so the earlier judgment did not bind her.

senses.head: Privity of contract — the warranty and third-party frame
examples: The subcontractor was never in privity with the owner and has to sue the general contractor instead.
Most states have dropped the rule that a buyer must be in privity with the manufacturer to bring a warranty claim.
The insurer is not in privity with the repair shop and cannot enforce the estimate against it.

senses.head: Privity of estate and of succession — leases, covenants, and preclusion
examples: The tenant is in privity of estate with the landlord for as long as the lease runs.
Because the assignee stands in privity with the original lessee, the covenant runs with the land.
The court held that the second plaintiff was not in privity with the first, so the earlier judgment did not bind her.

entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in PRIV-uh-tee with
entries.русский: юр. в договорных или иных правовых отношениях с — термин: между сторонами есть права и обязанности
entries.register: legal; a term of art. An American meets it in a warranty claim against a manufacturer, a lease or covenant dispute, or an opinion about whether an earlier judgment binds somebody — and essentially nowhere else. Outside law it reads as a malapropism for privy to.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a party — never a finite clause and never a gerund. In privity with buying the house is not English. What the two parties share is named with of inside the phrase rather than by a second complement: in privity of contract with the manufacturer, in privity of estate with the original lessee.
entries.pattern: be in privity with [party] · in privity of contract with [party] · in privity of estate with [party] · not in privity with [party] — the negative is the commoner form, because the point is usually that the plaintiff is a stranger to the deal
entries.variants: the bare noun takes of (privity of contract) or between (privity between the parties). The adjective privy to, meaning "let in on a secret," shares the Latin root and nothing else and is not this phrase.
entries.contrast: Not a comparison and not an alignment of opinion. It asserts that a legal relationship exists close enough for one party to enforce, or be bound by, what the other did. Against as between, which takes the relationship for granted and divides something up inside it, in privity with is the prior question of whether there is a relationship at all. Against being a party to a contract, which means you signed it, privity reaches successors who never did: a later buyer can be in privity with the original covenantor without having signed anything.
entries.see also: as between, as against, in conformity with, on behalf of, in violation of

entries.meaning: Names what an act, a document, or a body of evidence is backing. Unlike in favor of, which reports an opinion, this phrase attaches to something that was actually done.
examples: Two hundred people rallied in support of the striking nurses.
She testified in support of the bill at Thursday's hearing.
In support of the application, the college submitted four letters.
There is very little data in support of that claim.
The affidavit was filed in support of the motion to compel.
Two cutters were dispatched in support of the search.
Guard units deployed in support of the county's flood response.

senses.head: Backing a proposal, a cause, or a person
examples: Two hundred people rallied in support of the striking nurses.
She testified in support of the bill at Thursday's hearing.
In support of the application, the college submitted four letters.

senses.head: Offered as evidence for
examples: There is very little data in support of that claim.
The affidavit was filed in support of the motion to compel.

senses.head: Providing assistance to an operation — military and logistical
examples: Two cutters were dispatched in support of the search.
Guard units deployed in support of the county's flood response.

entries.русский: в поддержку; в подтверждение — о поступке, документе или доказательствах, а не просто о мнении
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in support of raising the minimum wage) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in support of [noun phrase] · In support of [noun phrase], [clause] · [document] in support of [motion] · evidence in support of [proposition]
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of in opposition to, and the two form the standard caption pair in American motion practice. Against in favor of, which states approval, in support of names something you are actively backing with an act, a document, or evidence: you are in favor of a bill, but you march in support of it. Against on behalf of, no authorization is implied.
entries.see also: in opposition to, in favor of, in defense of, on behalf of, on the side of

entries.meaning: Says two things are running together — on the same beat, the same schedule, or the same understanding. The metaphor is mechanical and reached general English from film and audio work, which is why it still fits best wherever timing is involved.
examples: Payroll is finally in sync with the new accounting calendar.
The two cameras have to stay in sync with each other to the frame.
Her instincts are in sync with what the neighborhood actually wants.
Wage growth is roughly in sync with inflation for the first time in three years.
Get your calendar in sync with the shared one before Monday.
The lights were never in sync with the traffic on that stretch of road.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɪð/ before a vowel · in SINK with
entries.русский: в такт с; синхронно с; заодно с — разг.: совпадение по ритму, графику или пониманию
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversational and technical, and increasingly at home in business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (in sync with him), or a free relative (in sync with what the rest of the team is doing) — never a finite clause and never a gerund. In sync with running the meeting is not English; write in sync with the way the meeting is run.
entries.pattern: [be/stay/get/fall] in sync with [noun phrase] · bring [X] in sync with [Y] · in sync — adverbial, no complement
entries.variants: in synch with is an accepted spelling and is losing ground; in sync is now the dominant American form. The full in synchronization with is technical and rare.
entries.contrast: The informal member of the conformity family. Against in line with, which reports that a figure matched a forecast, in sync with reports that two things are moving together in time or in intention — two departments can be in sync without ever having discussed anything. Against in agreement with, it is not about opinion at all. Its negative, out of sync with, is much the commoner of the two and is treated with the prepositions of contrast, exactly as inconsistent with is treated apart from consistent with.
entries.see also: out of sync with, in line with, consistent with, in keeping with, on a par with

entries.meaning: Names the person or body an actor is representing. It is the standard opening of formal remarks and the standard signature line of counsel and agents, and its core claim is agency: somebody else's interest is being carried.
examples: The attorney filed the motion on behalf of her client.
The union bargains on behalf of eleven thousand members.
He signed the lease on behalf of the corporation, not personally.
On behalf of the entire staff, thank you for twenty years.
He accepted the award on behalf of his late father.
Neighbors organized on behalf of a family that lost everything in the fire.
She has lobbied on behalf of rural hospitals for a decade.

senses.head: As the authorized agent or representative of
examples: The attorney filed the motion on behalf of her client.
The union bargains on behalf of eleven thousand members.
He signed the lease on behalf of the corporation, not personally.

senses.head: Speaking for a group ceremonially or courteously
examples: On behalf of the entire staff, thank you for twenty years.
He accepted the award on behalf of his late father.

senses.head: For the benefit of — the older in behalf of sense, now absorbed into this one
examples: Neighbors organized on behalf of a family that lost everything in the fire.
She has lobbied on behalf of rural hospitals for a decade.

entries.русский: от имени; в интересах кого-л. — говорящий или действующий выступает как представитель
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] on behalf of [noun phrase] · On behalf of [noun phrase], [clause] · on [possessive] behalf — the possessive frame
entries.variants: in behalf of was traditionally distinguished in American usage — on behalf of = "as the agent of," in behalf of = "for the benefit of" — but the distinction has collapsed and on behalf of now covers both. The reflexive is on my own behalf, never on behalf of myself. British usage is identical.
entries.contrast: Against for, this specifies representation rather than mere benefit: a lawyer files on behalf of a client, but you buy a gift for a friend. Against in the name of, which invokes an authority, on behalf of names a principal. Against in support of and in defense of, which require no authorization, this one implies that you were asked. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at on behalf of.
entries.see also: in support of, on the side of, in defense of, in the name of, for

entries.meaning: Names the camp you belong to. Sense 1 is about loyalty in a dispute; sense 2 is a frozen idiom for deliberate overcorrection, and it takes a virtue rather than a party as its object.
examples: The building inspector was plainly on the side of the developer.
The court came down on the side of the tenants.
Time is on the side of whoever can afford to wait longest.
He liked to say he was on the side of the angels, which nobody believed.
When in doubt, err on the side of caution.
The policy tells reporters to err on the side of disclosure.
She erred on the side of generosity in every estimate she ever made.

senses.head: Allied with; favoring in a dispute
examples: The building inspector was plainly on the side of the developer.
The court came down on the side of the tenants.
Time is on the side of whoever can afford to wait longest.
He liked to say he was on the side of the angels, which nobody believed.

senses.head: Err on the side of — deliberately overshooting a virtue
examples: When in doubt, err on the side of caution.
The policy tells reporters to err on the side of disclosure.
She erred on the side of generosity in every estimate she ever made.

entries.русский: на стороне кого-л. — в споре; в обороте err on the side of — сознательно склониться к (осторожности)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; in the err on the side of frame, an abstract noun naming a quality (caution, generosity, disclosure) — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: be on the side of [noun phrase] · come down on the side of [noun phrase] · err on the side of [quality] · on [possessive] side — the short frame
entries.variants: on X's side (history is on our side, the wind was on their side) is the ordinary short form. The literal spatial on the side of the hill is an ordinary of-phrase, not this preposition.
entries.contrast: Sense 1 declares an alliance and answers the question whose side are you on?. Sense 2, err on the side of, is a fixed idiom meaning "when in doubt, take too much of this rather than too little," and its complement is always a virtue, never a person. Against in favor of, sense 1 is about loyalty rather than about a position on a question; against in support of, it names a camp rather than an act.
entries.see also: in favor of, in support of, pro, on behalf of, with

entries.meaning: Declares the speaker on the same side as something. It is the shortest word in English for taking a position, which is exactly why it thrives as a prefix and struggles as a preposition.
examples: Nobody in that district is pro new taxes, whatever the polling says. (informal)
She's pro the merger but wants the timeline slowed down. (informal, British-flavored)
Pro-labor candidates swept the county races. (prefix — the normal American form)
The mayor is pro development in a way her predecessor never was.
We spent an hour on the pros and cons and settled nothing. (noun, not a preposition)
entries.русский: за; сторонник чего-л. — разг. и редк. как самостоятельный предлог; обычно приставка про-
entries.register: informal as a free-standing preposition and more current in British English than American; the prefixed form is neutral
entries.type: simple (marginal — from the Latin preposition; in American English overwhelmingly a prefix)
entries.complement: noun phrase only, usually bare (pro union, pro the merger) — never a clause, never a gerund. Distinguish the noun pro, meaning "a professional" or "an argument in favor" (the pros and cons), and the adjective (Is she pro or anti?), neither of which takes an object.
entries.pattern: be pro [noun phrase] · pro- [noun] as a prefix — the American norm · pro and con
entries.variants: American style hyphenates the prefix before a capital or wherever the closed form would be misread (pro-American, pro-labor). The Latin phrases pro bono, pro rata, pro forma, and pro tem carry their own Latin objects and are not this preposition in ordinary English use.
entries.contrast: The mirror of anti. Neither is fully naturalized as a free preposition in American English, where in favor of and against do the work. The frozen pair pro and con — from Latin pro et contra — has become a noun idiom (the pros and cons) rather than a prepositional one.
entries.see also: anti, in favor of, in support of, on the side of
